title: When to retire: the cultural evolution of post-reproductive oblique teaching
hypothesis: The hypothesis is most compelling when knowledge is costly to acquire and cheap to pass on.

Discussion




We have developed a model of a stage-structured population in which individuals are born into a hunting/reproducing stage and transition into a non-reproductive stage devoted to teaching, at a rate that is subject to selection.
The retirement rate determines what fraction of the population teaches, which improves hunter expertise, while the remaining individuals hunt and reproduce. We find that post-reproductive teaching can evolve in this setting, without either kinship or inclusive fitness. But it evolves only in populations larger than a threshold size.
Above this size threshold, the retirement rates that resist invasion form an interval rather than a point; and, often, the range of stable evolutionary outcomes sustain fewer teachers than would maximize the population’s intrinsic birth rate.






The retirement rate we study is a socially set schedule for ceasing to hunt and to reproduce, and not the physiological cessation of the reproductive system. Our results are accordingly not an account of menopause: the model makes no claim about the age at which reproduction becomes physiologically impossible, but only about when a society expects its members to stop hunting and reproducing, to begin instructing the young, and to be provisioned by those who still hunt. A norm of this kind is adopted by a group, not by an individual, set by social conventions about the age at which one stops hunting or gardening, expectations that the able-bodied provision the old, obligations of apprenticeship, and rules about who instructs the young. A type in our model is therefore a group that shares one such norm of social behavior. Norms and institutions of this kind can be understood as social technologies that a group adopts to sustain cooperation where individual incentives are insufficient 
(
Lie-Panis et al. 2024
; 
Lie-Panis et al. 2026
)
.






The unusual form of stable evolutionary outcomes in our model, an interval of stable phenotypes, follows from the dependence of a type’s fitness on the absolute size of the group that carries the trait.
In classical adaptive dynamics 
(
Geritz et al. 1998
; 
Åke Brännström et al. 2013
; 
OTTO and DAY 2011
)
, invasion fitness depends on the resident and mutant trait values alone; here it depends also on the founding population size of the mutant, because the rate at which amateurs acquire expertise depends on the absolute number of teachers they can reach.
A single mutant individual who retires earlier than all the residents gains nothing for its own type, because upon retirement it has nobody of the same type to instruct.

This size dependence, in both the initial population size and the size of the phenotypic change, confines our account to cultural rather than genetic evolution: a genetic mutation arises in one individual, whereas a group can adopt a substantially new norm for retirement and teaching in a single step

Henrich 2004

Our results provide a theoretical and evolutionary account of the information grandmother hypothesis, under which post-reproductive individuals repay their consumption by transmitting knowledge rather than calories 
(
Henrich and Henrich 2010
)
. That hypothesis, as originally stated, rests on relatedness: a grandmother is well placed to teach because her pupils are her descendants. Our model contains no relatedness by parentage, and therefore extends the hypothesis to oblique teaching by elders. What makes this extension possible is that unrelated individuals can nonetheless discriminate by type, namely by the norm of retirement they share: teachers instruct individuals of the same type, kin or not, and hunting returns are shared not with offspring but with anyone of the same type. The type with the greater expected lifetime return per individual then reproduces faster and comes to occupy more of the shared carrying capacity. The information grandmother hypothesis therefore does not require that the information be transmitted to kin; it requires only that the returns to expertise be shared among those who share similar norms for teaching and elder care.






Our findings complement existing theory on the evolution of teaching. Models of vertical and oblique transmission find that adding oblique transmission among non-kin makes teaching harder to evolve, because the benefit accrues to individuals who do not carry the teacher’s genes 
(
Aoki et al. 2017
; 
Mullon and Lehmann 2017
; 
Fogarty et al. 2011
)
. Our model does not contradict that conclusion. Those models describe a teaching trait spreading within a population; ours describes whole life histories competing for one environment, so that the benefit of an oblique teacher accrues to the teacher’s own type through the demography of the group rather than through descent. This account requires the assumption that the returns to expertise are shared across the population that generates them, as the benefits of specialization are shared in models of division of labor 
(
Michod 2007
; 
Cooper and West 2018
; 
Bell-Roberts et al. 2024
; 
Feinman 2011
)
.
The population threshold we obtain also connects our result to the literature on demographic prerequisites for cultural complexity 
(
Powell et al. 2009
; 
Shennan 2001
; 
Henrich 2004
)
.






We have focused on teaching and cultural evolution, but the structure of our result has a striking parallel in the evolution of complex organisms.
In multicellular organisms, a heritable change in developmental regulation can alter the fate of many functionally coordinated cells at once, so that sterile cells need not arise independently and spread one at a time

(
Gavrilets 2010
; 
Michod 2007
)
.
Theoretical work predicts that the advantage of non-reproductive somatic cells increases with the size of the collective 
(
Michod et al. 2006
; 
Michod 2007
; 
Zhang et al. 2026
)
, and that somatic cells are favored above a critical collective size when they improve the survival of the collective 
(
Zhang et al. 2026
)
.
Retirement into teaching is a similar division within a society: a non-reproductive class whose members raise the reproductive output of the rest, and which can be established by a group of sufficient size acting at once. Comparison between model predictions and empirical patterns of germ-soma division remains a topic for future research.






Our model has several limitations.
We do not model age itself: individuals retire at a constant rate, so the duration of the hunter stage is exponentially distributed.
We expect that fixing the age at retirement, rather than the rate, would shift the threshold

We also assume no relatedness whatsoever, which isolates the oblique case but understates the selection available in real populations; we speculate that adding relatedness between teacher and pupil would lower the threshold size

We treat expertise in a single skill, whereas a population transmits many skills whose returns may interact 
(
Smolla and Akçay 2023

Fogarty et al. 2015

Finally, we let only the retirement rate evolve and impose no constraint on the relationship between the total lifespan and the reproductive lifespan; holding the total lifespan fixed instead would correspond to the

One implication for the biological evolution of post-reproductive life follows from the cultural process we describe.
A norm under which individuals cease reproducing before reproductive senescence, and instruct the young instead, raises the value of surviving beyond the end of reproduction; and lower post-reproductive mortality in turn raises the fraction of teachers and, in the regime we analyzed, makes the return-maximizing retirement rate resistant to invasion.
Selection on genes affecting post-reproductive longevity would then act in an environment that culture has itself altered, which is the situation treated by theories of gene–culture coevolution 
(
Mullon and Lehmann 2017
)
.
We speculate that culturally evolved retirement contributed in this way to the post-reproductive longevity of humans; the mortality rates

The purpose of our simple model is not to give a quantitative account of retirement and teaching in any particular society, but to identify which factors govern how those characteristics evolve. Two factors are responsible here: hunting returns are shared among those who share cultural norms of teaching, and the benefit a teacher confers scales with the number of teachers rather than with their proportion. Wherever those two conditions hold, a stage of life spent teaching rather than hunting can be favored by selection among unrelated individuals, provided the population exceeds a threshold size.

Discussion




Phenotypic heterogeneity can fundamentally alter how populations organise collectively in space. In this work, we explored these effects using phenotype-structured nonlocal aggregation models, characterising how heterogeneity influences whether patterns form, how populations are distributed across phenotype space within them, and whether the resulting patterns are stationary or oscillatory. We considered interactions in which phenotype determines how strongly individuals produce signal and how strongly they respond to others. We analysed regimes in which phenotypic switching is slow and fast, providing useful bounds on the onset of pattern formation, before considering generic switching rates and showing how the linear growth rates interpolate monotonically between these limits.






A central result is that correlations between signal production and response strongly influence pattern formation. When individuals that produce stronger signals are also those that respond more strongly, pattern formation is promoted. Conversely, negative correlation, in which individuals specialise towards either signal production or response, inhibits pattern formation. Increasing phenotypic switching progressively dampens this effect: switching inhibits pattern formation under positive correlation but promotes it under negative correlation, with the distinction disappearing in the fast-switching limit.






Similar effects have recently been observed in a phenotype-structured Keller–Segel model 
[
31
]
. Under slow phenotypic switching, positive correlation between chemotactic sensitivity and chemoattractant secretion promotes pattern formation, whereas negative correlation inhibits it; under fast switching, the influence of these correlations again disappears. The emergence of the same qualitative behaviour in a different aggregation framework suggests that our insights may have broader generality.






We also characterised how patterns are structured in phenotype space. Under slow switching, this structure follows the response function: more responsive individuals become more concentrated at the centre of an aggregate, while less responsive individuals remain more spatially dispersed. In contrast, signal production has no effect on the phenotype structure of the pattern. Increasing phenotypic switching progressively homogenises this structure until, in the fast-switching limit, the pattern becomes uniform across phenotype space. An important consequence is that aggregation is collective: weakly interacting individuals that could not pattern in isolation can nevertheless be recruited into an aggregate through their interactions with the wider population. This extends even to individuals whose interactions are repulsive.






Another theme of this study is how phenotypic complexity can be introduced, and under what conditions this leads to spatio-temporal oscillations.
 Generally in interacting systems, increasing the number of components can lead to increasingly complex eigenvalue spectra and dynamical behaviour. For example, Turing-Hopf (wave) instabilities in standard reaction–diffusion systems require three or more components 
[
47
]
, while work on complex ecological systems has demonstrated how stability depends on both the number and structure of interactions 
[
32
, 
2
]
. This raises an interesting challenge in contexts such as developmental patterning, where the desired outcome is often a stable spatial structure whilst populations contain substantial phenotypic complexity.






Our results provide several examples of interaction structures that 
can maintain stationary patterns even with substantial phenotypic complexity.
 If all 
cross-phenotype
 interactions are attractive, the leading eigenvalue is always real, so spatio-temporal oscillations cannot arise through linear instability, even in the presence of phenotypic switching. Even if some interactions are repulsive, sufficiently fast switching can homogenise the phenotypes to behave effectively as one, preventing oscillatory linear instabilities. Finally, under slow or negligible switching, response–signal separation similarly gives only real pattern-forming growth rates. This leaves the possibility for spatio-temporal oscillations under response–signal separation only when some 
cross-phenotype
 interactions are repulsive, sufficient attraction remains to drive pattern formation, and phenotypic switching occurs on a comparable timescale to movement in physical space. Indeed, under these conditions we observe spatio-temporal behaviour arising through both linear and fully nonlinear mechanisms. 
In the nonlinear case, we observe a nucleation–merging mechanism similar to that seen in previous models 
[
38
, 
36
, 
24
]
. However, the underlying mechanism appears to be novel, driven by switching between attractive and repulsive phenotypes rather than proliferation. Both the linear and nonlinear spatio-temporal behaviour discussed above are examples of how movement in phenotype and physical space can couple to continually restructure patterns in both spaces.






Other interaction structures can similarly restrict oscillatory behaviour; for example, 
detailed balance
 between species interactions can give rise to gradient-flow structures 
[
7
]
. More broadly, identifying interaction structures that constrain oscillatory dynamics may help to explain how complex heterogeneous populations maintain stationary spatial organisation.






Throughout this study, we considered both discrete and continuous phenotype formulations, each offering distinct mathematical advantages. The continuous formulation naturally lends itself to PDE and continuum methods, as illustrated by our calculation in Section 
6.1
 for generic switching rates. The discrete formulation is more general, applying for arbitrary 
N
N
 without requiring interactions to vary smoothly with phenotype, while also allowing the use of finite-dimensional matrix methods. For systems with many discrete phenotypes, this formulation may additionally open the door to random matrix theory, which has long been used to relate the spectra of large interaction matrices to ecological complexity and stability 
[
32
, 
2
, 
39
, 
4
, 
5
]
. Our results highlight the benefits of considering both formulations, allowing whichever mathematical tools are most 
straightforward
 for a given problem to be used.






There are many compelling directions for future work. In Part II 
[
26
]
, the follow-up to this work, we will move from interactions that depend on absolute phenotype to those that depend on phenotypic distance, allowing interaction strength to depend on how similar individuals are to one another. Beyond this, our treatment of phenotypic switching as 
homogeneous
 linear diffusion is a simplification. Studies of epithelial–mesenchymal plasticity have shown that phenotypic states can differ substantially in their stability and transition properties 
[
22
]
, motivating phenotype-dependent switching rates. Nonlocal switching kernels provide another natural extension, allowing transitions between distant phenotypes 
[
12
]
. Incorporating phenotype-dependent proliferation and death would be particularly relevant for modelling cancer, where proliferation, migration and phenotypic state can be strongly coupled 
[
41
]

Conclusion




In this work, we have taken significant steps on the way to assess the unitarity and causality of Asymptotically Safe Quantum Gravity. Gravitational scattering amplitudes are a prime target in this endeavour. For the concrete example of the gravitational scattering of scalar fields, we provided an approximation of the scalar-scalar-graviton vertex, including the full momentum dependence in all tensorial channels.






We find that starting from the fixed point, we can derive fully analytic, or simple Feynman-parameter integral, representations for the physical vertex functions. While the computation relies on Euclidean signature, the high degree of analytic control allows a straightforward analytic continuation to Lorentzian momentum configurations. For the on-shell configuration relevant to scattering, we find the expected branch cut structure along the imaginary graviton momentum axis.






A key finding is that, once the differing mass dimensions of the form factors are accounted for, all form factors contribute quantitatively approximately equally. In other words, we find that non-minimal operators 
cannot
 be neglected in Asymptotically Safe Quantum Gravity.






Our approximation is under control best for small momenta. Here, we find the expected soft double-eikonal divergences predicted by the Weinberg soft theorem 
[
31
]
. This is remarkable as along the 
RG
 flow, our setup breaks diffeomorphism symmetry due to regularisation and gauge-fixing. Nevertheless, the soft divergences computed in our setup are diffeomorphism-invariant and reproduce the correct numerical prefactor.






The high degree of analytic control comes at a price, however. For large momenta, we find that neglecting the self-feedback of the vertex introduces a leading-order error, in line with the findings of a previous numerical computation of the same vertex 
[
22
]
. In such a numerical setup, resolving the soft terms is more challenging though.






This leads us to a clear conclusion for how correlation functions should be computed. Analytic approximations as discussed here and in 
[
23
, 
24
]
 provide information about the analytic structure of correlation functions, which are particularly relevant for 
IR
 physics. These then inform fully numerical setups in a number of ways: they identify the numerically most important channels (in our case, all of them) as well as where branch cuts are expected. The numerical setup then needs to take into account a self-consistent closure to accommodate the high-momentum limit correctly.






There are some technical barriers which have to be overcome in the future to make our analytic framework applicable to a wider range of theories. First, the specific choice of the regulator shape function that allows the explicit evaluation of threshold integrals only works straightforwardly for gapless theories. A first extension should thus generalise the framework to gapped theories. Second, due to their different kinetic structure, fermions need a separate treatment, and a simple shape function as used here might not straightforwardly lead to similar analytic results.






Our results can be systematically extended to compute other vertex functions. The clear next target is the four-scalar vertex, extending 
[
23
]

Conclusion




In this study, we presented a comprehensive empirical investigation into the effectiveness of snapshot testing in front-end development, utilizing both quantitative data from 340 GitHub repositories and qualitative insights from a survey of 60 experienced practitioners.
Our mixed-methods analysis reveals that integrating snapshots significantly boosts median statement coverage to 86.7% and increases mutant detection by over 1.3 times. Practitioners appreciate snapshot testing for its low implementation cost and its efficacy in catching Program Anomaly (70.0%) and GUI (53.3%) defects, which can often identify issues that standard assertions miss. However, snapshot testing also faces significant challenges, including high cognitive load during reviews, false positives during intentional updates, and flakiness caused by non-deterministic values (

Future work should focus on developing techniques to improve the reviewability of snapshot differences and mitigate the fragility associated with large snapshot files.

hypothesis:
After the election, Better Markets pressed the same point, calling bettors “mostly young males” who “are not and never will be a statistically valid sample of likely voters” 
(
Kelleher, 2024

. This paper tests that criticism with anonymized trade-level data from Kalshi, a CFTC-regulated exchange and the largest regulated political prediction market to date in the United States.
conclusion:
7 
Conclusion




This paper examines the relationship between demographic diversity and forecasting accuracy in political prediction markets. The paper has three findings.






First, the premise of the diversity critique is correct. Kalshi’s trader base was predominantly young and male, a demographic profile far from that of the electorate whose behavior the market was forecasting.






Second, the predicted consequence never materialized. Kalshi’s prices, like those of Polymarket, the Betfair exchange, and the bookmakers, were more accurate than every poll-based forecaster in the national race. Kalshi was more accurate than every poll-based forecaster in the battleground states and Senate races, and less accurate than FiveThirtyEight only in the thinly traded House districts. No poll-based model would have profited by trading against Kalshi’s prices in any presidential contest group, and the markets correctly priced Trump as the favorite while poll-based models treated the race as a coin flip.






Third, the mechanism that reconciles these facts is financial incentives. The cohort of traders whose behavior most resembles political expression was 73% long Harris and had the lowest returns. The cohort that dominates dollar volume was 64% long Trump, had the highest returns, and, through the two-sided traders who supply most of its volume, bought at prices that proved on average fair. Under fractional partisan attribution by the home zip code’s 2024 vote, the partisan gap in dollar-weighted trade direction falls from roughly seven percentage points among casual traders to zero among the traders with more than 100 trades who set prices, and the partisan gap in profitability declines in the same way. Trading profit is unrelated to sex, and among traders with more than 100 trades the direction of trades does not differ significantly by sex or age. The association of profit with geography and with age disappears once the side the trader took is accounted for. Formally, the price distortion that selected participation can produce is the product of a selection gap and the dependence of beliefs on type at the dollar-weighted margin. The gap is large, the association between politics and the direction of trades is not distinguishable from zero where volume concentrates, and on geography the gap has the opposite sign from the one the critics assume. The data is inconsistent with a model in which traders buy the outcome they prefer and consistent with one in which the market price reflects the beliefs of the marginal informed trader, the mechanism 
Forsythe et al. (1992)
 conjectured for the Iowa Electronic Markets and which our evidence confirms directly.






These findings challenge the widely held view, popularized by 
Surowiecki (2004)
, that demographic diversity is necessary for accurate collective judgment.








In prediction markets, demographic diversity is overruled by financial incentives. More generally, our analysis supports the claim that the structure of the institution in which a group operates matters more than the composition of the group.








The findings also answer the most common criticism leveled at prediction markets in 2024. Critics who inferred biased prices from an unrepresentative trader base were implicitly assuming that traders’ positions follow their identities. The evidence rejects that assumption, and a century of evidence from demographically narrow, persistently accurate election markets suggests that the market mechanism does not require representative participants. A regulated exchange open to the public, in its first month of election trading, produced prices that were more accurate than every poll-based forecast and that were not noticeably biased by the inferred political preferences of its traders.

Discussion




We have proposed baRRR, which integrates bidimensionally linked data by decomposing variation into covariate-driven and auxiliary low-rank modules, each of which may be shared across any subset of sources and cohorts. The framework contains maRRR and BIDIFAC+ as special cases, and its algorithms impute entrywise and blockwise missing data as part of the fit. In simulations, baRRR recovered both shared and individual-level signal and had the lowest imputation error for every class of missing entry, including samples with all outcomes missing, where imputation amounts to predicting outcomes from covariates. In the TCGA application, auxiliary structure accounted for most of the variation, while mutation-driven variation was concentrated in modules spanning small groups of cancer types, such as the module shared by ovarian and uterine cancers, rather than in pan-cancer structure.






Several limitations point to future work. First, the module structure must be specified in advance, so it would be hard for larger views or cohorts since there can be a lot of combinations; we took it from BIDIFAC+ applied to the same data, so module-level interpretations are conditional on that selection, and a procedure that selects modules jointly with the covariate effects would be preferable. Second, our penalty weights are fixed by a random matrix argument and an empirical Bayes approach in the spirit of

Other directions include formal inference on which mutations drive each module, statistical error bounds and convergence rates for the estimator, and nonlinear extensions. baRRR models both covariate effects and auxiliary structure as linear and low rank; deep learning approaches to multi-view integration

(

(

This paper offers a unified treatment of many classic models of disclosure, integrating all frictions into a single object: a specification of privately observed disclosure costs, realized only when the firm chooses to disclose. The framework encompasses most commonly-used models of voluntary disclosure and yields generalizable intuitions that can be tested empirically, without requiring the selection of specific, and potentially unobservable, aspects of the theory. In particular, we prove that disclosure is decreasing in the frictions, increasing in fundamental uncertainty, and that greater uncertainty about disclosure costs reduces disclosure when the cost uncertainty is sufficiently large. Put differently, the framework provides a novel perspective on evidence games, akin to noisy signaling models, where the firm observes two private signals, fundamentals and costs, but can only communicate a single-dimensional information (see, e.g., 
?

?

This study extends the EVT-based risk-aware reinforcement learning framework considered in the baseline methodology to policies parameterized by neural networks. The main limitation of the original approach in this setting arises from its reliance on finite-difference gradients, whose computational cost increases with the number of policy parameters. Conclusion and Future Work




Video generation looks increasingly realistic, yet its physical plausibility remains poorly measured. Existing evaluations rely on semantic binary judgments or camera-centric geometry, and cannot reduce physical plausibility to computable, testable quantities. We propose PVBench, a physical-quantity-driven benchmark that extracts numerical measurements with specialized vision models, checks them against physical laws, uses same-scene T2V/I2V paired prompts, and resorts to MLLM scoring only for hard-to-quantify dimensions. Our key finding is that numerical physical-quantity scores are more discriminative than MLLM semantic scores and highly consistent with human judgments, enabling more reliable and quantifiable evaluation. Limitations and Future Work.
 The evaluation depends on specialized vision models and skips only a small number of samples for unobservable cases; material and phase-change dimensions still use MLLM scoring. We only ablate the VLM backend, and a full ablation of the specialized evaluators is left for future work. Moreover, the current evaluation largely relies on checking consistency with physical laws and, except for a few dimensions, lacks ground-truth references. More robust tracking and finer physical quantities will improve coverage. In future work, we plan to build ground-truth references for conditional image-to-video (CI2V) models using physics engines and other simulation tools to enable more direct evaluation. This paper studies the spread a liquidity provider requires to break even against orders that can exploit an outdated quote. That spread depends on two features of the trading arrangement: the time for which the quote remains binding as the reference price moves and the maker’s ability to reject informed orders, and we place these two protections on a single scale. The competitive half-spread is the unique spread at which revenue from uninformed flow covers the expected excess of the stale-price innovation over the spread, weighted by the ratio of admitted informed to uninformed flow. Shortening the horizon lowers that expected excess at every spread, screening lowers the ratio, and Theorem 
1

The comparison requires only an integrable innovation, so it holds with jumps, atoms, and infinite variance.






Three theoretical results shape how the threshold should be read. First, it is scale-free and converges, as informed flow becomes rare, to one minus the ratio of expected absolute innovations at the two horizons, which under Gaussian innovations is one minus the square root of the horizon ratio. Second, its response to toxicity is governed by the expected loss per executed informed order rather than by aggregate loss. Convexity orders aggregate losses across horizons but not this conditional severity, so in general the threshold can fall as toxicity rises. The Gaussian case is what delivers a threshold that increases with toxicity, together with lower executed volume for the screened maker at the matching spread. Third, at equal horizons, screening narrows the spread by strictly less than the screening rate times the unscreened spread, because the narrower spread makes additional informed opportunities profitable.






Predictable drift is a centering problem rather than a spread problem. When the quote is held at the current reference, drift raises the break-even spread, at second order near zero drift under Gaussian innovations and linearly in the exposure horizon when residual uncertainty vanishes. In the Gaussian low-toxicity limit, it raises the required screening from one minus the square root of the horizon ratio toward one minus the horizon ratio itself as drift comes to dominate diffusion. 16

title: A tutorial on quantum scattering theory and coupled-channel calculations of bimolecular collisions
hypothesis:
We aim to state all conventions, such as normalisation, phases and index ordering,
as explicitly as possible, allowing each step to be followed and verified.
conclusion:
Conclusions




In this tutorial we have gone from the most general form of a Hamiltonian for two interacting particles to a full description
of setting up a quantum simulation of the collision.
To this end, we introduced the Born-Oppenheimer approximation, effectively separating the electronic problem from the problem of colliding nuclei.
We then exploited the translational invariance of the system to separate out the centre-of-mass motion.
By expanding the wavefunction in terms of asymptotic states and inserting it into the Schrödinger equation,
we arrived at the coupled channel differential equations.






Next, we introduced the asymptotic boundary conditions in terms of Riccati–Bessel and Riccati–Hankel functions,
which solve the differential equation in the absence of the interaction potential but still accounting for the
centrifugal term.
Critically, it was seen that the relative (complex) amplitudes of the incoming and outgoing Riccati–Hankel functions encode
the information required to extract physically observable information such as the 
𝐒
\mathbf{S}
-matrix as
well as differential and integral cross sections.






Taking a first step in the direction of a numerical treatment of the quantum scattering problem,
we then regarded the simple case of two structureless particles colliding, by only accounting for
a single quantum channel.
For this special case we saw how the scattering amplitude relates directly to the cross section
and how the scattering phase can be used to express several scalar quantities.
Through Taylor-expansion of the solution, we derived Numerov’s method for solving second order differential
equations and saw how the stability could be improved by propagating the ratio of the solution in neighbouring points.






Finally, the tutorial culminates in a full quantum treatment of an atom-diatom system.
To this end we introduced the Jacobi coordinate system and, together with an expansion in the
diatomic and angular bases, reduced the problem to a set of coupled one-dimensional equations.
We saw how another numerical technique, the discrete variable representation could be used to
obtain eigenvalues and eigenstates of the diatomic molecule which were needed to evaluate the
interaction potential matrix elements as a function of the interparticle distance.
We then generalised Numerov’s method to work with multichannel systems, which can be used to obtain
the reactance matrix from the propagation.
We saw how to obtain the 
𝐒
\mathbf{S}
-matrix from the open-open block of 
𝐊
\mathbf{K}
, leading to the Arthurs–Dalgarno
expression for the integral cross section. Since total angular momentum and parity are conserved, the scattering problem
segments into numerically manageable blocks.






Hopefully, this tutorial will have covered many of the pitfalls and fuzzy areas that beginners
in scattering theory often have to deal with and which many textbooks tend not to cover in detail.
Throughout, we have tried to build a consistent bridge between quantum mechanical theory
and numerics.
Whilst it would be impossible to give every single detail, the philosophy of this tutorial is
to be as explicit as possible, chaining together concepts to build a coherent picture.
To name just a few, we have paid special attention to the basis states and the coordinates they
are associated with.
We have also seen what consequences the choice of unit amplitude versus unit flux normalisation
has for the formulation of observables, and how to go from one form to the other.
Further, paying attention to the ordering of matrix indices (rows=channels, columns=solutions) turned
out to be critically important for the physical interpretation of simulations.
Equipped with this framework, we expect the reader to be able to not just implement the relevant
equations in code but also be able to apply physical intuition in order to interpret results.






In order to keep the scope of this tutorial finite, certain topics were only briefly addressed
or even omitted entirely.
Reactive collisions, for example, require a way of modelling the breaking of a bond and the
creation of another, for instance by performing coupled channel simulations with a hyperspherical
coordinate system
[
49
]
, or can be treated with fundamentally different methods such as time-dependent
wavepackets
[
50
]
.
We have not considered the effects that external fields have on our collisions, which makes
the derivations slightly more complex but is possible to do in principle as shown in Krems’
textbook 
[
3
]
.
Another huge topic, that was taken entirely for granted is that of potential energy surfaces.
In practice obtaining these is a numerically very demanding process, whilst also requiring a
high degree of expertise to obtain good results.
Even once individual points have been obtained, there is an art to fitting them to make a
continuous surface which can be sampled at arbitrary points, such as using the
reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS) method 
[
17
, 
18
]
.






Readers who have taken a foray into the world of collision simulations using this tutorial
thus have a springboard towards new topics, with plenty of directions to go in.
As computational capabilities grow, so too will the sizes and variety of systems to explore.
For production calculations, readers may also turn to established, well-tested packages such as MOLSCAT 
[
5

6

across contexts reflect these structural features, reflecting a reorganization of how content

7. Conclusion 
We have argued that awakening is best understood not as a transient altered state 
but as a trait-level organization of the global structure of experience: a durable shift in how 
mental contents are appropriated, reacted to, and evaluated, rather than a change in the 
contents themselves. The present account, grounded in the enactive framework, 
reconceives awakening as a transformation in the relational dynamics of cognition. By 
linking phenomenological reports to candidate processes of co -emergence and 
dereification, it offers a path toward bridging subjective experience and objective 
measurement, opening the door to systematic empirical investigation. 
Testing this framework will require moving beyond a single assessment modality. 
Structured phenomenological interviews, such as the micro-phenomenological approach 
developed by Petitmengin (2006, 2017), are one candidate of which promise Trautwein et 
al. (2024) illustrate directly. Their effects tracked interview-based rather than self-report 
measures of self-dissolution, addressing the structural limitation of self-report identified in 
Section 4. Experience sampling, which probes experience repeatedly in real time across 
everyday contexts rather than relying on a single retrospective report, would speak more 
directly to the proposed context-independence of the changes. Informant reports offer 
another useful source of evidence because they do not depend on the same self-referential 
processes under investigation. Ideally, these measures would converge with behavioral or 
task-based indices of the four dimensions defined in Section 3, allowing the framework to 
be tested across several partially independent sources of evidence rather than through any 
one measure alone. Such task-based indices still need to be developed, and to our 
knowledge, no existing assessment approach combines phenomenological, ecological, 
third-person, and behavioral evidence in the way required here. Future work should look 
into specifying and validating such an assessment stack as a necessary next step for testing 
the account proposed here.

index—the mean of the dereification distribution—which, combined with an index of 
transition flexibility across states (its mobility), provides a minimal, two -part 
operationalization to be validated convergently against the neural and interview measures 
noted here. We present this scheme as illustrative rather than as a validated instrument.

title: Sorption Molecular Dynamics of Point Defects in 2D Materials with a Machine Learning Potential
hypothesis: In this work, we investigate whether the machine learning interatomic potential MACE can reproduce sorption trends (adsorption vs. absorption) previously obtained from high-throughput DFT calculations and extend the analysis to elevated temperatures. One such approach involves introducing dopant atoms through sorption, the process by which atoms or molecules are taken up by a material through either absorption or adsorption. Here, we investigate whether single dopant atoms occupy interstitial sites within the 2D material (absorption) or bind to its surface (adsorption).
conclusion:
Conclusion




The results show that MACE can reproduce the general DFT trends for adsorption versus absorption in doped 2D materials, while requiring only a fraction of the computational cost, making the method suitable as a high-throughput screening tool for identifying promising defect–host combinations before performing more expensive DFT calculations.






The overall sorption trends remain largely unchanged at 300 K despite thermal activation, indicating that the energetic preference for adsorption is robust for most investigated systems. At the same time, the finite-temperature simulations reveal thermally activated defect migration and other stability effects that cannot be captured by static 0 K calculations alone. The inclusion of finite-temperature effects enables the investigation of defect behavior under more realistic operating conditions and may reveal temperature-induced trends that are inaccessible in conventional high-throughput 0 K DFT studies, demonstrating the potential of machine-learning interatomic potentials for efficient large-scale finite-temperature studies of defects in 2D materials.






Overall, the presented approach demonstrates that machine-learning interatomic potentials can substantially expand the scope of computational defect studies while retaining the qualitative sorption trends obtained from DFT.

title: EEG Correlates of Verbal and Perceptual Reasoning
hypothesis:
Modern DTI research also 
corroborates the brain myelination hypothesis of intelligence (Miller, 1994). Penke et al. 
(2012) investigated 12 white matter tracts that together explained 12% of variance in 
6 
 
FSIQ, supporting the hypothesis that white matter integrity is related to speed and 
efficiency of cognitive processing.
conclusion:
16 
 
DISCUSSION 
 
This study explored possible correlations between the EEG variables of individual alpha 
peak frequency (IAPF), relative alpha power (8-12Hz, averaged across electrodes), and 
10-12Hz alpha coherence between electrodes Fp1-P3 and Fp2-P4 in eyes closed and 
eyes open conditions, with scores on a measure of verbal reasoning (Cattell Verbal IIIB) 
and a measure of perceptual reasoning (Cattell Culture Fair), and also explored possible 
effects of all three EEG variables on each of the two Cattell test scores. 
 
No significant relationship was found between IAPF and either Cattell test.  This finding 
did not replicate previous research (e.g. Anokhin & Vogel, 1996; Doppelmayr et al., 2002; 
Klimesch, 1999; Polunina & Davydov, 2006), which found a positive relationship between 
IAPF and IQ.  All IAPF values were within the expected range of 7.5-12.5Hz (Klimesch, 
1999), although two participants had an EEG profile that fit the “low amplitude fast” 
phenotype, a normal variant pattern dominated by low amplitude beta-wave activity with 
no discernible alpha peak (Gunkelman, 2001).  Heart rate variability scores were within 
expected ranges for fit, healthy adults, where higher scores indicate higher 
parasympathetic activity and low scores can be indicative of anxiety and stress.  
Partialling out HRV scores to control for physiological arousal (as a proxy for trait anxiety) 
had a negligible effect on IAPF/IQ correlations, suggesting that participants’ physiological 
arousal levels were fairly similar across the group. 
 
There was also no significant relationship between either Cattell test and relative alpha 
power, which again did not replicate previous research (e.g. Jausovec, 1996; Langer et 
al., 2011; Polunina & Davydov, 2006; Thatcher & Lubar, 2005) where a relationship 
between relative alpha power and IQ had been identified.  This study examined combined 
alpha from the alpha1 (8-10Hz) and alpha2 (10-12Hz) bandwidths; a more fine-grained 
analysis of the individual EEG frequencies may render different results.  Furthermore, 
relative power was used to control for the wide age range of the participants, since alpha 
power changes over the lifespan (Klimesch et al., 2000).  However, Thatcher and Lubar 
(2005) found smaller effect sizes of relative power than absolute power when looking for 
EEG/IQ correlations.  However, participants of similar age would need to be recruited if 
using absolute EEG power as the power variable. 
 
17 
 
Furthermore, no significant relationships were found between either Cattell test and 10-
12Hz alpha coherence, except for one positive correlation between CFIT scores and 
coherence at electrodes Fp1-P3 in the eyes-closed condition.  This single positive 
relationship contradicted previous research that reported negative correlations between 
coherence and IQ (Neubauer & Fink, 2009; Thatcher & Lubar, 2005) but supported the 
findings of Yang and Chaou (2005) and Lee et al. (2012) who reported positive 
correlations.  It is difficult to interpret this single result given the number of other 
nonsignificant findings, but Jung and Haier (2007) reported greater left hemispheric 
activation for some P-FIT areas so, if meaningful, this finding would imply greater parietal-
frontal left-hemisphere upper alpha connectivity is related to higher perceptual reasoning 
ability.  Since most of the findings were very clearly not significant, no post-hoc correction 
for multiple comparisons was carried out as it seemed unlikely such would alter the 
results, but it remains possible that this single positive correlation was a chance finding.  
Again, a more refined analysis of single EEG frequencies may render a different result. 
 
Multiple regressions to explore possible correlations between all three EEG variables and, 
separately, the two Cattell tests did not find any significant relationships, a finding which 
did not replicate the multiple regression by Thatcher and Lubar (2005) which identified 
some dozen or so EEG variables modestly to strongly correlated with intelligence.  
Thatcher and Lubar, however, used a very large number of predictor variables that they 
had also checked using discriminant analyses between high and low IQ samples and 
there may have been large differences in statistical analysis techniques between Thatcher 
and Lubar and the current study. 
 
In view of the foregoing, the experimental hypotheses that relationships would exist 
between the EEG variables and verbal and perceptual reasoning scores were not 
supported by the data and were rejected.  The lack of replication of previous findings, 
however, may have been because this study differed in several ways (participants, 
psychometric tests, and design) that cumulatively may have had an effect on the overall 
findings. 
 
Because of the small number of available participants, it was not possible to select for 
handedness or sex; however, score differences between the sexes were nonsignificant.  
On the other hand, it was possible to control for age, in the EEG data by using relative 
rather than absolute alpha power (Klimesch et al., 2000), while the Cattell tests are age-
18 
 
normed (Cattell & Cattell, 1960a; 1960b).  It is also possible that the nonsignificant 
findings are linked to the very atypical mean IQ scores of the participants.  Because of 
recruitment difficulties in the average IQ range, more than half the participants had IQs 
>2SD above the population mean.  The findings therefore cannot be generalised to the 
wider population. 
 
Detterman and Daniel (1989) established that psychometric variables correlate less well in 
HIA populations and render a “spikier” cognitive profile.  Furthermore, it is known that HIA 
individuals tend to score lower on processing speed relative to other cognitive domains 
(Watkins, Greenwall & Marcell, 2002).  This finding implies that speed no longer relates to 
cognitive “power” beyond a certain IQ level and, if included in a battery composite, may 
drag FSIQ down.  The Cattell tests are administered under very tightly-timed conditions, 
and it has been suggested that highly-speeded test administration may introduce 
construct-irrelevant sources of variance (Lu & Sireci, 2007).  The irrelevance of speed in 
an above-average IQ group was supported by a notable ceiling effect on the VCPT task, 
with most participants making few or zero mistakes, and demonstrating reaction times and 
reaction time variability faster than the norms for their age group. 
 
Previous research also typically used either a Wechsler battery (to derive FSIQ) or 
Raven’s Matrices (as a proxy for g).  The current study, on the other hand, used tests of 
verbal and perceptual reasoning, rather than a composite IQ score.  Continued research 
emphasis on a unitary structure for intelligence has meant that little neuroscientific 
investigation has been conducted into first and second order CHC theory factors (Stankov, 
2017).  To identify the neural underpinnings of “intelligence in general” rather than 
“general intelligence” (Colom et al., 2002), these lower order factors will need to be 
investigated thoroughly.  To date, there has been too little functional imaging work using 
HIA participants to fully clarify the neural mechanisms of very high IQ.  Specific imaging 
and/or EEG work in HIA populations will be required, along with the use of a more 
sophisticated cognitive test, preferably a full battery with a low speed loading, with 
extended norms for valid measurements in the high range. 
 
In terms of design, most literature reviewed for this study looked for differences between 
groups of participants assigned by IQ level.  It may have been easier to obtain a 
significant result comparing groups with smaller numbers of participants, whereas this 
19 
 
study used a correlational and regressional design which, ideally, would have benefited 
from a larger sample size. 
 
Given the foregoing, therefore, the lack of significant findings in the current study should 
be treated with caution and not necessarily be interpreted as contradicting any previous 
EEG and imaging studies or existing theory of intelligence.  It is proposed that, just as 
psychometric g weakens and eventually unravels completely in HIA populations, so that 
high psychometric performance relies increasingly on specialised abilities (Spearman, 
1927), if there is such construct as a “neuro-g”, the neural processes giving rise to it also 
cease to correlate well with higher intelligence, with high performance brains becoming 
increasingly neurologically specialised.  Haier (2009) pointed out that psychometric g may 
not correspond in a unitary fashion with brain structure.  Certainly, the neural processes 
underpinning individual WAIS task performance remain poorly understood (Polunina & 
Davydov, 2006).  However, research to date suggests that the neural underpinnings of 
intelligence map somewhat better onto two dimensions (Nisbett et al., 2012) rather than 
one.  The strongest support so far has been for the distinction between fluid and 
crystallised intelligence (Horn & McArdle, 2007), hence building on the current study’s 
exploration of verbal and perceptual abilities seems a reasonable starting point. 
 
Other variables were obtained during data collection that could not be analysed in the 
current study due to their number and complexity, and it is possible that a more 
comprehensive evaluation of the recorded data may more fully elucidate the relationships 
between the EEG measures and IQ scores.  Event-related potentials recorded during the 
VCPT task were not analysed and these data may reveal greater relationships with the IQ 
scores than the resting EEG alone.  Although 10-12Hz alpha was the waveband most 
strongly correlated with FSIQ or g in the literature, it remains an open question how 
different EEG frequencies correlate with first- and second-order CHC factors.  This study 
examined coherence patterns at four electrode sites (Fp1-P3 and Fp2-P4); it was not 
feasible to investigate all 171 possible pairings.  There is a suggestion that different 
patterns of activation occur between short-range networks and long-range connections 
(Thatcher et al., 2016).  Furthermore, that Jung and Haier’s 2007 review also suggested 
some P-FIT regions activated bilaterally while others showed more prominent left 
hemispheric activation merits additional follow-up.  Future research should focus on 
addressing the methodological limitations of the current study previously described, and 
20 
 
also exploring the additional variables that were identified but could not be analysed in this 
study. 
 
Given the substantial work still needed to connect psychometric measures with their 
neural foundations, it is unlikely that “neuro-metrics” will replace psychometrics in the 
foreseeable future.  The field of “differential neuroscience” (Deary, 2012) is still very much 
in its infancy.  It is envisaged that as this psychometric/neuroimaging research 
progresses, a new paradigm will eventually emerge connecting the CHC theory 
expounded by Carroll (1993) and Jung and Haier’s (2007) P-FIT model, which will serve 
as the basis of future experimental imaging work in the field of intelligence.  However, any 
new theoretical intelligence framework will need to possess sufficient predictive validity 
and reliability to measure all the way to the extremes of the ability scale to be useful in 
furthering our understanding of very high intelligence. 
 
To summarise, this study sought to explore the relationships between the EEG variables 
of individual alpha peak frequency, relative alpha power, and alpha coherence, and 
measures of verbal and perceptual reasoning.  The findings generally were not significant 
and did not accord with earlier research findings on EEG and IQ.  However, no previous 
EEG study included such a large proportion of high intellectual ability participants, who 
may have considerably different psychometric and neurological profiles to the majority of 
the population and the findings cannot be generalised.  Furthermore, this study highlighted 
many EEG and cognitive variables that remain thus far unexamined.  Finally, attention is 
drawn to the need for future intelligence research to work towards connecting existing 
psychometric and neuroscientific paradigms.

title: Robust Real-Time Monocular Human Pose Estimation with Insole-Based Sensor Fusion
hypothesis: In these challenging but common scenarios, vision-only systems often struggle to reconstruct physically plausible lower-limb motion and reliable foot-ground contact. Due to the highly unobtrusive and wearable nature of smart insoles, this paper investigates whether simple plantar pressure and acceleration sensors can effectively resolve these visually induced limitations.
conclusion:
Conclusion and Future Work




This paper presented a part-decoupled vision–pressure–inertial fusion framework for real-time monocular human pose estimation. We investigated whether sparse plantar-pressure and foot-acceleration signals can provide complementary cues when monocular visual evidence is incomplete or unavailable. The framework maps heterogeneous visual observations into a unified root-relative skeleton space, incorporates foot sensing into lower-body temporal modeling, and uses a lightweight global coordinator to maintain whole-body consistency.






Experimental results show that the insole-enhanced framework improves pose accuracy and temporal smoothness over vision-only temporal baselines under clean conditions, with larger gains under lower-body occlusion. Analysis of short visual dropouts further demonstrates the value of continuous foot-contact and foot-dynamic cues. The method also improves contact-sensitive gait measurements, including stance accuracy, step-distance error, and cadence error. These results indicate that sparse pressure–inertial foot sensing provides useful physical priors for robust human motion estimation.






Although the experiments use I-SOL smart insoles, the formulation only assumes synchronized sparse plantar-pressure and foot-mounted acceleration streams with comparable temporal resolution. The method is therefore not limited to a specific insole model. Data organization, action definitions, and preprocessing scripts will be released to support reproducibility.






The method nevertheless has several limitations. First, it estimates root-relative pose rather than long-term global trajectories. Because the current sensing setup lacks reliable global orientation, extended visual dropouts may still cause drift. Second, broader evaluation across users, environments, and motion types is needed. Third, downstream applications such as ergonomic risk assessment, rehabilitation scoring, and abnormal gait screening require further validation.






Future work will improve long-horizon robustness through lightweight global motion constraints and explicit contact-state modeling. We will also explore mobile and edge deployment with real-time visual front-ends and Bluetooth insole streams, and extend evaluation to industrial monitoring, home rehabilitation, and long-term daily activity assessment.

The main limitation of the present model is its phenomenological nature. Our aim was not to construct a quantitatively fitted representation of cortico-limbic physiology, but rather a proof-of-principle framework for asking how the temporal integration of stress memory can alter effective interactions between prefrontal and amygdala populations, and thereby reshape the resulting dynamics. The functional forms used to represent these interactions were therefore chosen to be as simple as possible while reproducing the qualitative mechanisms of interest. Likewise, the parameterization was guided by known relationships, relative strengths, and physiological constraints reported in the empirical literature, but the exact numerical values were not fitted to data and should not be interpreted as direct physiological measurements. Where possible, we considered parameter ranges compatible with these qualitative constraints and searched within those ranges for the dynamical phenomena of interest. Hence the specific numerical boundaries of the oscillatory and non-oscillatory regimes should be interpreted as model-dependent, with the same applying for the transitions and mechanisms identified here as the main predictions of the framework.






A second limitation is that the modeled circuit is intentionally incomplete. We focused on a minimal prefrontal-amygdala system in order to isolate the consequences of stress-sensitive modulation of recurrent cortical excitation and amygdala inhibition. Emotion regulation, however, emerges from a considerably larger network. The hippocampus, thalamic and hypothalamic structures, neuromodulatory systems, and the HPA axis itself can all contribute to the production, interpretation, and regulation of stress responses. In the present formulation, the influence of these omitted systems is absorbed only indirectly into effective coupling terms, tonic inputs, or the delayed modulation imposed on the cortico-limbic circuit. The model should therefore be viewed as an open subsystem embedded within a substantially larger physiological network rather than as a closed representation of stress regulation.






A related limitation is the absence of direct empirical validation of the model’s dynamical predictions. At present, there are no data that simultaneously resolve the evolving cortico-limbic population dynamics and the temporally distributed effects of cortisol with sufficient temporal detail to identify the type of history-dependent interaction represented here. This lack of data is in part the motivation for the present modeling approach. One goal of such models is to identify which measurements would be most informative, and to generate hypotheses about how delayed hormonal modulation should alter neural dynamics under different baseline circuit conditions. Future experimental and modeling work could therefore proceed iteratively: models can suggest specific temporal relationships and parameter dependencies to measure, while new physiological and imaging data can in turn constrain the functional forms, parameter ranges, and delay structures used in the models.






More broadly, understanding how the time course of cortisol action interacts with emotion regulation remains an important and incompletely resolved problem. Cortisol production and action occur within a much wider physiological context and are influenced by factors such as sleep, age, broader hormonal state, autonomic regulation, cardiovascular function, and previous stress exposure. 38

This paper develops a discrete-time survival model that incorporates a dynamic industrial graph to capture the joint evolution of latent risk and cross-area dependence. The motivation is that geographic proximity captures only one dimension of regional dependence: areas that are geographically distant may nevertheless be exposed to similar mortgage risk when they share comparable industrial compositions. Industrial similarity therefore provides an alternative basis for identifying economically connected areas. However, these relationships are not necessarily stable, as changes in local industrial composition may cause previously similar areas to diverge and previously dissimilar areas to become more closely connected. A model based on a fixed graph cannot capture such changes, even if the associated latent effects are allowed to vary over time, since the set of connections through which dependence is represented remains unchanged. Therefore, it may continue to impose dependence between areas that are no longer economically similar while failing to recognise newly emerging relationships.






We address this limitation by reconstructing the industrial graph annually from contemporaneous industrial composition, allowing both its topology and edge weights to evolve over time. The resulting sequence of graphs determines the cross-area dependence of annual latent effects, while a first-order autoregressive process links the latent effects across successive years. We jointly combine these two components within a proper conditional autoregressive framework, with explicit conditions ensuring the validity and identifiability of the proposed model. Estimation is performed using the Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation, which exploits the sparsity of the joint precision matrix to accommodate a large panel of mortgage observations. We evaluate the proposed model using U.S. mortgage data, comparing a baseline specification with models based on static and dynamic industrial graphs.






The empirical analysis yields four main findings. First, industrial similarity provides a meaningful basis for representing cross-area dependence in mortgage default risk. The high estimated structure weights in both the static and dynamic industrial specifications indicate that graph-induced cross-area dependence plays an important role in explaining residual variation beyond observed borrower and loan characteristics. Second, the estimated persistent value further indicates substantial temporal persistence in latent risk, while allowing the effects of annually updated industrial graphs to enter through new innovations. Third, allowing the graph to evolve improves model performance beyond what can be achieved with a fixed graph. The dynamic specification achieves the lowest DIC and WAIC and the highest LPML, suggesting that changes in industrial relationships contain information about mortgage default risk that is not fully captured by static connections. Fourth, the improvement extends beyond in-sample fit to out-of-sample prediction, achieving the highest AUC and KS statistic, indicating stronger discrimination for defaulting loans.

First, the graph is currently constructed from contemporaneous industrial composition; incorporating forward-looking information, such as announced plant openings and closures, or patent filings, could improve both the timing and the accuracy of graph updates. Second, edge formation and dissolution could be modelled explicitly using dynamic stochastic block models or temporal exponential random graph models, which would provide edge-level uncertainty and distinguish edge disappearance from edge weakening. Discussion




We introduced a mathematical framework to the modeling of epidemiological time series via branching process theory and PGFs.
It allows us to systematically extract joint probability distributions for general outcome of oubreaks over time, derived from the state of the epidemic or its incidence in the population, like cases or hospital admissions.
Being fully analytical, our framework enable efficient computation for inference and prediction of epidemics evolution, two key applications of outbreak analytics.
We demonstrated the operational practicality of our framework through both synthetic experiments and an application to the modeling of influenza hospital admission.






Here, we limited ourselves to age-stratified epidemic models for simplicity, but the approach is straightforward to generalize to integrate more sociodemographic and socioeconomic features. It can also describe spatial dynamics through metapopulation approaches 
[
69
, 
70
]
, enabling the modeling of importation and detection of pathogens from travelers 
[
29
]
. Future work should formalize the encoding and extraction of such time series within our PGF framework.






When faced with sufficiently high-dimensional observables, we leveraged the CGF to approximate the underlying the joint probability distribution over observables.
Since we limited ourselves to second-order moment matching, the resulting predictions and inferences performance should be similar, in principle, to techniques like Kalman Filtering and linear noise approximations 
[
71
, 
72
, 
55
, 
44
]
.
However, let us highlight that the multivariate PGF encapsulates the full discrete stochastic process.
Hence, any improvement to extracting the underlying distribution—while remaining computationally feasible—would enhance the predictions of this framework.






While we limited our inference experiments to a limited number of parameters, our framework is general and readily applicable to inference tasks in higher dimension. For instance, time-varying reproduction number estimation 
[
73
, 
74
, 
75
]
 is an active area in the epidemic modeling community.
In this context, semi-mechanistic renewal models are most often used, which share many of the assumptions of branching process and PGF evaluation, but the set of tools and methods employed are different.
A thorough assessment of PGF inference, benchmarked against current methods and software, would help clarify where PGF modeling stands relative to other approaches in computational epidemiology.






Finally, we foresee many applications and future avenues for the improvement of PGF-based forecasts.
Predictions in the early growth phase of an epidemic or at the beginning of an influenza season could leverage PGF models similar to the one used here.
Posterior inference could be used to seed or constrain the parameter space exploration performed by complex simulation-based models.
Another direction is to to extend the applicability of our approach past the initial growth phase by developing explicit modeling of immunity in the population.

hypothesis: These studies provide the foundation for modeling sarcasm directly, but they also motivate asking how sarcasm interacts with other NLP tasks that depend on speaker intent. Thus, this study shifts the focus from sarcasm classification to investigating its broader effects; specifically, we examine whether sarcasm creates a hidden failure mode in the safety-critical domain of hate speech detection.
conclusion:
6 
Conclusion




In this paper, we presented SarcasTraps: Effect of Sarcasm on Turkish Hate Speech Detection. In the set, each example is annotated for both hate speech and sarcasm, yielding four conditions that separate literal hate, non-hateful sarcasm, and sarcastically expressed hate. This design allows us to evaluate not only whether models detect hate speech in general, but also whether they remain reliable when harmful intent is expressed indirectly.






Experiments with BERTurk and XLM-RoBERTa classifiers trained on existing Turkish hate speech datasets, evaluated across five random seeds, as well as zero-shot LLMs, show that sarcasm exposes a systematic weakness in current hate speech detection systems. Fine-tuned encoder-based models tend to miss sarcastically expressed hate, while zero-shot LLMs retain higher recall on sarcastic hate but also produce more false positives on non-hateful sarcastic examples. These results indicate that sarcasm affects hate speech detection in different ways across model families and that standard evaluation settings can obscure these failures.






Overall, SarcasTraps demonstrates that sarcasm is not only a phenomenon to be detected on its own. It is also a factor that can affect model behavior in safety-critical tasks. It shows that robust hate speech detection requires models to distinguish not only harmful from non-harmful language, but also literal harmfulness from indirectly expressed group-directed hostility.








7 
Limitations




SarcasTraps is designed as a targeted test set for evaluating the effect of sarcasm on Turkish hate speech detection systems. It contains 479 examples, which limits the scale of the quantitative evaluation. This size is partly due to the difficulty of finding naturally occurring examples that simultaneously involve hate speech and sarcasm. While hateful language and sarcastic language are both common in informal online discourse, examples where the two interact clearly enough to support reliable annotation are much rarer. For this reason, the results should be interpreted as evidence from a targeted test set.






Another limitation is the class distribution of the set. Because Ekşi Sözlük is organized around titles, data collection required identifying relevant titles and then selecting entries under those titles. To obtain enough hateful examples, we intentionally inspected titles where hate speech was more likely to occur, such as discussions involving socially or politically salient target groups. As a result, SarcasTraps contains more hateful than non-hateful examples. This imbalance reflects the targeted purpose of the dataset, but it also means that the set does not represent the natural prevalence of hate speech or sarcasm.






Future work can extend SarcasTraps by adding more examples and covering additional target domains beyond the ones considered in this study. A larger and more diverse benchmark would allow more fine-grained analyses. Another important direction is the development of sarcasm-aware hate speech detection systems. The results in this paper suggest that models trained on standard hate speech datasets are not sufficient for robustly handling sarcastically expressed hate, so future systems may benefit from sarcasm detection signals, or multi-task learning setups that jointly consider sarcasm and hate speech.






Finally, future work should examine whether context improves hate speech detection in sarcastic cases. Prior work showed that title-level context can help sarcasm detection in Ekşi Sözlük-style discourse. A natural next step is to investigate whether similar title-level or discussion-level context can also improve the detection of hateful intent when it is expressed indirectly through sarcasm. Such work could clarify whether failures on sarcastic hate are caused primarily by missing pragmatic cues in the entry itself, or by the absence of broader contextual information about the title, event, or target group being discussed.






Because SarcasTraps focuses on hate speech and informal online discourse, it contains sensitive and harmful language that is not censored in order to preserve the original content.








8 
Ethical Considerations




This study aims to support research on sarcasm-aware hate speech detection in Turkish online discourse. Because SarcasTraps focuses on hate speech and informal online discourse, it contains sensitive and harmful language that is not censored in order to preserve the original content.






SarcasTraps is constructed from naturally occurring entries on Ekşi Sözlük and is intended solely as a research resource for analyzing how sarcasm affects hate speech detection systems. The dataset should not be used to amplify hateful content or to target individuals or communities as the set itself may cause harm if redistributed without restrictions, or used outside of its intended research purpose.






All examples were collected by the authors. The examples were independently annotated by three native Turkish speakers: the two authors and an Turkish MSc student from the same laborator y who is not an author. The annotators are native Turkish speakers who are familiar with Ekşi Sözlük discourse and the goals of the project. The annotators were not recruited through a crowdsourcing platform and did not receive payment.
We do not report protected demographic attributes of annotators, beyond task-relevant information such as native Turkish proficiency and familiarity with Ekşi Sözlük discourse.
Before collection and annotation, they were informed that the data would contain hateful, offensive, and disturbing content. During annotation, they focused only on two specific dimensions: whether an entry contains hate speech and whether it is sarcastic. They did not evaluate the political correctness, factual accuracy, moral acceptability, or ideological position of the entries.






Because the set was constructed from a public source, and the collection followed the platform’s robots.txt restrictions, no formal ethics review was obtained for this study. We do not release the set as a public download; instead, access will be provided only upon request for academic-only purposes.
The dataset contains only the title, entry content, hate label, and sarcasm label. We do not collect or release usernames, timestamps, profile information, or other metadata that could be used to identify Ekşi Sözlük authors to reduce privacy risks. We did not obtain individual consent from Ekşi Sözlük users, as the entries were collected from publicly accessible pages. We acknowledge that public data does not always translate to consent for research 
Fiesler and Proferes (2018)
. As suggested in  
(
Fiesler and Proferes, 2018
)
, we are not mass gathering entries from specific people. The titles and entries in the set do not include any identifying information. We masked individual person names appearing in the entries, but all the other content remains uncensored. Due to sensitive nature of the data, SarcasTraps will be distributed only upon academic request under research-only terms.






Large language models were used as zero-shot classifiers in the experiments; they were not used to generate SarcasTraps entries or assign the annotations. We used ChatGPT 5.6 and Grammarly to check spelling and text flow after drafting our own version, and incorporated suggestions for more appropriate wording.

title: XForecast: The KDD 2026 Finance Day Challenge on News-Grounded Financial Forecasting
hypothesis: We host the XForecast Challenge on Kaggle as part of KDD 2026 Finance Day, providing a standardized evaluation protocol and leaderboard benchmark. Through this benchmark and competition, we aim to encourage research on multimodal financial forecasting and advance methods that more effectively integrate financial TS data with textual information.

6 
Conclusion




We introduce XForecast, a benchmark and competition for news-grounded financial forecasting that integrates financial time-series data with curated textual signals. By combining structured financial texts generated using FinTexTS with historical stock price data, the dataset enables systematic evaluation of how financial news can be leveraged for stock price forecasting. The challenge focuses on predicting stock price movements four weeks ahead for 100 large-cap companies, with a realistic temporal split between training and evaluation periods. To better assess models that effectively utilize textual signals, we propose a weighted hit rate evaluation metric that emphasizes instances where news information is expected to have a stronger influence.

The inspected solutions covered diffusion models, inverted Transformers, temporal neural networks, tree ensembles, and foundation-model-based tabular methods, while frequently combining market-wide and stock-specific signals. Beyond leaderboard performance, the post-competition review underscores the importance of precise temporal constraints, unambiguous text-use policies, and reproducible execution environments. We hope this benchmark encourages further research on multimodal financial forecasting and advances methods that effectively integrate numerical market data with textual information.

We begin with the closed-loop result, because it matters most for deployment. A judge denied the
material its subject had to respect is not, in a repair loop, an inexpensive approximation of an

same rules govern the agent that produced the output, so the world given to an agent should be
evaluated along with what the agent did with it. Our claim is scoped to corpora in which the

important property is that the trigger for that reorganisation lies inside the regulator. A quarterly
