Indeed, it is worth remarking that the interval analysed here lies close to solar maximum, when the heliospheric current sheet is highly warped and the global coronal magnetic field evolves comparatively rapidly. One might therefore expect intrinsic coronal evolution to substantially degrade the performance of the static approximation. Instead, our results demonstrate that, over timescales of approximately a solar rotation, the large-scale projected density distribution remains sufficiently stable that the resulting “static” backgrounds are qualitatively similar to those obtained from the fully time-dependent simulation. Whether this conclusion also holds during solar minimum remains to be determined—the streamer belt is considerably less warped and evolves significantly more slowly during that phase of the solar cycle, suggesting that static approximations may perform even better, although the overall simpler heliospheric current sheet morphology may also alter the relative contributions of individual structures to the constructed backgrounds.










5 
Summary and conclusions




In this work, we have investigated the extent to which background subtraction applied to white-light coronagraph observations inadvertently subtracts K-coronal signal together with the intended F-corona contribution. Under the idealised assumption of a perfectly removed F-corona, any residual signal incorporated into the constructed backgrounds originates solely from the K-corona. We have exploited this scenario by analysing synthetic white-light imagery derived from the 32-day, near-real-time, data-assimilative MHD simulation of 
Downs et al. (2025)
, which contains only the K-coronal component. This allows, for the first time, a direct quantification of the effects of background subtraction against a known ground truth.






We have employed three input data sets (time-dependent tB, time-dependent pB, and static tB) together with four background construction methods (minimum of daily medians, Med, and direct minimum, Min, each applied over 15- and 29-day windows) to evaluate the impact of background subtraction over the three-day interval for which all backgrounds could be generated. We find that the overall morphology of the K-corona is remarkably well preserved following background subtraction. The largest coronal structures, including streamers, pseudostreamers, and open-field regions, remain readily identifiable, although quantitative analyses reveal systematic changes in both the absolute and relative brightness of different structures.






We found that constructing backgrounds over a 29-day window, as is commonly done for real coronagraph observations, consistently removes less total K-coronal signal and generally provides a more faithful recovery of the relative brightness distribution of coronal structures than the corresponding 15-day backgrounds. This demonstrates that sampling approximately one full solar rotation provides a more robust estimate of the background, despite the greater amount of intrinsic coronal evolution encompassed by the longer interval. Furthermore, we found that background subtraction applied to pB imagery removes systematically less K-coronal signal than for tB (by approximately 5%), although the corresponding tB images generally preserve the relative brightness distribution of coronal structures slightly more faithfully.






We also noted that, although the Min method removes less total K-coronal signal than Med by construction, the two approaches perform similarly in preserving the relative brightness of streamers, pseudostreamers, and open-field regions. This is an encouraging result, as practical background subtraction applied to real coronagraph observations must rely on Med-like approaches to mitigate the influence of instrumental noise, cosmic ray hits, and other image artifacts, which would otherwise have a disproportionate impact on backgrounds constructed using the direct minimum. Since the synthetic observations analysed here are free from such effects, 
the relative performance of the Med and Min methods under more realistic observing conditions remains to be investigated.






An additional noteworthy result is that backgrounds constructed from synthetic coronagraph images generated by “flying” a virtual spacecraft through a single static 3D MHD solution reproduce many of the characteristics derived from the fully time-dependent simulation. Despite the absence of intrinsic coronal evolution, the resulting backgrounds exhibit qualitatively similar morphology and quantitatively comparable performance in terms of both signal loss and structural preservation. In fact, our comparison with the underlying 3D coronal density showed that, although the streamer belt undergoes continuous intrinsic evolution, the large-scale projected density distribution remains sufficiently stable over multiple days that the same rarefied coronal structures continue to dominate the constructed backgrounds. Although this result has no direct analogue for real coronagraph observations, it has important implications for numerical modelling. In particular, it suggests that, for many applications, steady-state coronal models combined with realistic observing geometries may provide a practical and computationally inexpensive tool for generating high-fidelity synthetic coronagraph imagery that can be processed in the same way as real observations, thus enabling more direct and meaningful comparisons.






Finally, we emphasise that the interval analysed in this work corresponds to the near-maximum phase of the solar cycle, during which the heliospheric current sheet is highly warped and the large-scale coronal magnetic field evolves relatively rapidly. Despite these intrinsically dynamic conditions, the background subtraction methods examined here preserve the overall morphology of the K-corona remarkably well over the three-day interval considered. Whether the quantitative results reported here depend on the phase of the solar cycle remains an open question. Although the slower intrinsic evolution of the corona during solar minimum might intuitively be expected to improve the performance of background subtraction, the much flatter heliospheric current sheet means that the streamer belt remains confined to a relatively narrow range of PAs over a solar rotation. Consequently, the balance between dense streamer regions and projected open-field regions contributing to the constructed backgrounds may differ substantially from the solar maximum conditions investigated here. A similar analysis during solar minimum would therefore provide valuable insight into the extent to which the conclusions presented here depend on the global coronal magnetic configuration and its time-dependent evolution.






Overall, our results demonstrate that the large-scale morphology of the K-corona remains largely intact following background subtraction, although its photometric properties are inevitably modified to varying degrees. Quantifying these effects is therefore essential for studies that rely on the absolute or relative brightness of coronal structures. 
An important limitation of the present study is that the synthetic observations contain only the K-corona and do not account for the effects of the overlying F-corona on background construction and subtraction. While this idealised setup allowed us to isolate the impact of background removal on the K-coronal signal, the results do not capture the full complexity of processing real coronagraph data. Building on the foundation laid by this work, our next step will be to incorporate a modelled F-corona into the MHD-generated synthetic imagery, allowing us to investigate how the combined K- and F-coronal signals affect background construction and subtraction, and how these effects may differ from those found for the “dust-free” corona analysed here. We will then introduce additional sources of image degradation, including random noise, missing pixels, and instrumental artifacts. This stepwise approach will allow us to test the background subtraction procedure under progressively more realistic observing conditions, while quantifying simultaneously how effectively the F-corona is removed and how much K-coronal signal is lost in the process.

Discussion




We have addressed two shortcomings from our original work 
(
Klobusicky et al., 2020
)
 on the analysis of cooperative transport of two molecular motors which could be of the same type (homogenous ensemble) or different types (heterogenous ensembles). The first, addressed in Section 
6
, concerns the model for the relation between detachment rates of the motor and the instantaneous force it experiences. In our previous work as well as others 
(
Bovyn et al., 2020
; 
Bovyn et al., 2021
)
, this was modeled by some version of a direct fit to the data from 
Milic et al. (2017)
; 
Milic et al. (2014)
; 
Andreasson et al. (2015a)
 which relates detachment rates (inferred from measured run lengths and velocities) to the applied trap force. This neglects the effects of fluctuations in the instantaneous force, and also leads to a discontinuity or sharp transition in the detachment rate as the force on the motor switches from the hindering to the assisting direction. Applying a model with this sharp transition in detachment rates leads to grossly inaccurate behavior at low hindering or zero trap forces due to force fluctuations into the assisting force direction which dramatically accelerates detachment. A similar artefact of a discontinuous detachment rate model is shown for gliding assay models in 
Hou and Kramer (2026)
. We addressed this inconsistency by simply fitting the data from 
Milic et al. (2017)
; 
Milic et al. (2014)
; 
Andreasson et al. (2015a)

The parameterized fit for the instantaneous force-detachment rate based on single molecular motor runs of kinesin-1 and kinesin-2 are then used self-consistently for the instantaneous force-detachment rate relation in our forward predictions for ensembles of two motors.






More recent experiments on the relationship between detachment rates and forces on molecular motors have pointed to the importance of considering both the longitudinal force (parallel to the microtubule) and transverse force (perpendicular to the microtubule) on the motor. In optical trap assays such as the experimental data we reference 
(
Milic et al., 2017
; 
Milic et al., 2014
; 
Andreasson et al., 2015a
)
, the cargo tends to be rather large (hundreds of nanometers) relative to the motor so trap forces applied longitudinally also induce substantial transverse forces. In other experimental configurations where the transverse force is reduced, the dependence of the detachment rate on the applied longitudinal force appears to be qualitatively different. In particular, the detachment rate is found in 
Khataee and Howard (2019)
; 
Noell et al. (2026)
 but not in 
Hensley and Yildiz (2026)
 to exhibit catch bond rather than slip bond behavior, meaning the detachment rate actually decreases with applied longitudinal force when in the hindering direction. In cells, we do not expect the large cargos and large transverse forces typical of conventional optical trap assays, and thus these more recent experiments are likely to be more informative about how molecular motors including kinesin work in the cell. We are not aware, though, of studies with reduced transverse force that map out a simply parameterized relationship between detachment rates and applied forces as cleanly and comprehensively as in 
Milic et al. (2017)
; 
Milic et al. (2014)
; 
Andreasson et al. (2015a)

1

in vitro

Our framework should however be adaptable in principle to other experimental configurations with reduced transverse forces provided we have available a sufficiently rich measurement of detachment rates (or run lengths and velocities) as a function of longitudinal force. We could retain our one-dimensional structure by using the approach in 
Hou and Kramer (2026)
 of leaving the transverse force implicitly dependent on the longitudinal force via geometric relations presented in 
Pyrpassopoulos et al. (2020)

(
Noell et al., 2026
)
. If data became available to model the detachment rate jointly as a function of longitudinal force and transverse force, it could be incorporated into our modeling framework provided we extended the model for the cargo variable to be at least two-dimensional or fully three-dimensional. This would not be difficult to do by maintaining the cargo as a point particle in higher dimensions, but a proper accounting of the geometry in two or three dimensions would track the dynamics of the point of attachment of the motor to the cargo, as done theoretically in 
(
Choudhary et al., 2026
)

(
Erickson et al., 2011
; 
Nguyen et al., 2024
)

The other unrealistic simplification in the model from 
Klobusicky et al. (2020)

(
Arpağ et al., 2019
; 
Arpağ et al., 2014
; 
Bovyn et al., 2021
; 
Erickson et al., 2011
; 
Kunwar et al., 2008
; 
Takshak and Kunwar, 2016
; 
Furuta et al., 2013

Korn et al., 2009
; 
Nguyen et al., 2024

Klobusicky et al. (2020)

In particular, we had assumed the dynamics of the motors is fast compared to the attachment/detachment time scale, which is true for kinesin-1 and kinesin-2 in 
in vitro

To address this, we relaxed the assumption that the relative separation of the two motors, in the 2AM state where they are both attached, reaches the stationary distribution before detachment is likely to occur. We decomposed this 2AM state into a lax phase where at least one motor has a slack tether and a taut phase where the tethers of both motors to the cargo are engaged. The nature of these phases depends on whether the properties of the two motors create true cooperativity in the sense of leading to load-sharing or whether they tend toward opposition. Accordingly, the taut phase can be analyzed either in terms of quickly reaching a stationary distribution or of quickly leading to detachment via a semi-deterministic approximation. The lax phase can be analyzed in terms of constant drift and diffusivity of the motors within this phase.

Conclusion




This study integrated EL222-regulated optogenetic expression, light-associated stress, and macroscopic bioprocess dynamics into a compact mechanistic model. Ensemble-based parameter estimation was combined with 
a posteriori
 screening for locally stable intracellular steady states, reflecting the assumed long-term intracellular behaviour under reference light conditions. This generated an ensemble of biologically plausible parameterisations consistent with the available experimental data, model structure, and screening criteria. The ensemble predictions captured the main experimental trends, while variability across parameter estimates and predicted trajectories highlighted the range of possible behaviours that would be overlooked by selecting a single fitted parameter set. Future work will focus on developing tailored model-based reinforcement learning and Bayesian optimisation approaches to optimise optogenetic protein production under phototoxicity. These approaches will explicitly account for parameter uncertainty in process optimisation and control-policy design.

Since our replicability metrics are computed from draws of the hierarchical model, they also partly measure shrinkage.
We have discussed why we adopt a hierarchical model: since we are studying the replicability between studies that derive from the same super-population, the assumption that the studies are dependent is reasonable, and shrinkage embodies it, borrowing strength that also stabilizes the metrics for small studies. It further allows us to compute all the generative metrics, and thus to address the important question, discussed above, of the relationship between replicability and meta-analysis. (

)

;

;

For a given SNP–transcription factor pair, there is typically no prior meta-analysis from which to read off a plausible heterogeneity, so this route is unavailable in its literal form. What the genome offers instead is a large universe of biologically analogous regulatory relationships: many other pairs whose effects have been measured across studies, and whose between-study variability can be characterized even when a specific pair has not been studied enough to support a meta-analysis. \tau_{\beta}

\tau

(

(

donors used in the analysis, we still prefer a pool of similar biological pairs to standard generic priors, because genomics provides a large set of comparable relationships from which plausible, realistic values for the effect of interest can be obtained. Assessing Replicability without a Prespecified Threshold




The proposed replicability metrics rely on the prespecified threshold 
ε
\varepsilon
 that defines the region of practical relevance. Trying different thresholds 
ε
\varepsilon
 requires no refitting: the metrics are recomputed from the existing posterior draws.






Ideally, the threshold should be set independently of the data, on the basis of scientific judgment. Yet, in truly novel contexts where such information is absent, the framework can be read through summaries without a prespecified boundary. One could examine the posterior distribution of the difference between the study-specific effects, for example, between the largest and smallest ones, or summarize how far the posterior distributions of the study-specific effects overlap.






We kept the main analysis anchored to the single threshold 
ε
\varepsilon

https://github.com/esteralongi/The-Quantification-Of-Replicability
).








7.4 
Replicability across Many Studies




Our development has kept the number of studies 
S
S
 small. However, it is worth asking how the framework behaves as 
S
S
 grows. The replicability questions that we discussed scale naturally. With the consensus level 
k
k
, we can already measure replicability within subsets of studies rather than across all of them, which helps especially when the collection grows. Inference on the generative effect becomes more reliable as more studies inform it; and the predictive questions persist in both directions, since the accumulated evidence can be used prospectively to forecast a future study, or in a leave-one-out setting, holding out each study in turn to assess retrospective replicability across the collection.






However, the joint metrics presuppose that the studies are exchangeable members of one super-population, an assumption more easily violated when 
S
S
 is large, since the collection may then contain clusters of studies. Thus, it could be worth assessing exchangeability jointly with the replicability analysis; this idea has been formalized in related settings through Bayesian nonparametric models that embed clustering and model comparison in a single joint framework 
(
Trippa et al., 2015
)
. In our framework, one might fit the generative model on all studies except one and check how well the held-out study agrees with it.






Even within a subset of studies, one could assess replicability pairwise, two studies at a time, as in the Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology 
(
Errington et al., 2021
)
, rather than jointly. The two are not interchangeable, and the choice can change the conclusions. 
Ganzfried et al. (2013)
 illustrate this difference concretely with the prognostic role of 
CXCL12
 expression in ovarian cancer: the association with survival emerged from the combined analysis of many studies, in only a few of which the gene was individually a significant predictor. A pairwise assessment would register very few successes, since most pairs contain no two individually significant studies. However, the combined analysis finds a coherent signal precisely because it accumulates evidence that individual studies, each too small on its own, cannot provide alone, even if it can be driven by a minority of studies. Therefore, pairwise and joint assessments answer different questions, and the choice between them should be based on the scientific goal.






Together, these considerations suggest a richer extension of our framework to the many-study setting. However, a full development lies beyond the scope of this article, whose primary aim is to introduce a new conceptualization of replicability; we leave it to future work.








7.5 
Extension to More Parameters




We have illustrated our work through a linear regression in which a single coefficient 
β
\beta
 is the object of interest, in order to present the framework as clearly as possible. However, neither the model nor the parameter is essential. The framework rests only on a generative model and on joint posterior probabilities, and nothing requires a single coefficient: a model with additional covariates and several coefficients of interest is still handled, because replicability is still assessed through the same posterior probabilities over a region of practical relevance, applied to each coefficient. When several coefficients are of joint interest, that region can be applied to each of them marginally or specified jointly in the parameter space.








7.6 
The File Drawer Problem




“The journals are filled with the 5% of the studies that show Type I errors, while the file drawers back at the lab are filled with the 95% of the studies that show nonsignificant results.” 
(
Rosenthal, 1979
)
. As early as in 1979, Robert Rosenthal discussed a well-known problem that remains open today: a collection of published studies may represent a selected subset of all the studies actually carried out. This phenomenon, now commonly called 
publication bias
, can distort the distribution of the observed study-specific effects and, consequently, the assessment of replicability based on them.






In our empirical application, there is no publication bias in the choice of the studies: the studies are observed independently of the parameters that generated them. Since we defined the studies by taking the ancestral groups from the entire GTEx dataset, they are not selected based on some criterion of significance of their effects.






When feasible, preregistered multi-lab studies, including multi-lab Registered Reports 
(
Nosek and Lakens, 2014
)
, provide a natural prospective setting for our framework. In Registered Reports, the research questions, study design, and analysis plan are peer-reviewed before data collection, and the publication decision is made primarily on the basis of the proposed questions and methods rather than on the direction or statistical significance of the results. This substantially reduces the outcome-dependent selection of studies underlying publication bias. Therefore, although such coordinated designs are not always feasible and do not replace retrospective analyses of existing evidence, they offer a promising direction for assessing replicability transparently from the outset.






If, instead, one wanted to assess the replicability of effects from already published studies, the probability that a study is observed may depend on its results, and so it would be necessary to take publication bias into account. In the meta-analysis literature, several methods for correcting this bias have been proposed; 
Haaf (2020)
 provides a review of these methods.






In the framework of replicability that we proposed here, one could leverage the fact that a generative model fully specifies the process that produces the studies, and can therefore be extended by introducing an explicit selection mechanism, as 
Bayarri and DeGroot (1987)
 proposed. By modifying the generative model so that it also generates the data that end up in the file drawer because of their nonsignificant results, one could then apply the replicability framework we proposed, computing the proposed metrics with respect to the latent population of conducted studies rather than only the observed subset. This would make it possible to distinguish replicability within the available evidence from the replicability expected across the broader process that generated the studies.








7.7 
Broader Applicability




Although we have illustrated the framework through an application in genomics, its architecture is independent of that specific domain: it applies to any field that combines evidence across studies sharing a common super-population, for example through a hierarchical structure. Multi-site clinical trials, large-scale replication projects in psychology and the social sciences, and multi-laboratory experiments all share study-specific effects related to one another through a common generative effect. In each of these settings, the metrics would quantify the replicability of the effects of interest, revealing not only whether the studies replicate but also why, by examining the joint and conditional probabilities linking the generative effect, the study-specific effects, and their heterogeneity.
The framework provides a systematic assessment of replicability before broad scientific claims are drawn. When replicability is lacking, it further makes it possible to investigate its source and, where useful, to inform the design of a new study.

Conclusion




FLEX option activity in the filtered single-name universe is best understood as an observable institutional-demand marker. It identifies names with high listed implied volatility, coincides with changes in regular listed-option open interest, and reveals volatility-carry conditions when listed IV is high relative to recent realized volatility. It is not, in this sample, a stable directional equity-return signal or a fully executable trading system.






The central implication is that FLEX should be studied as part of the listed-option market structure, not only as a bespoke product category. FLEX contracts are negotiated outside the regular standardized chain, but their risk is managed in an ecosystem that includes listed options and equities. The paper’s evidence is consistent with that ecosystem view. A useful analogy is to think of FLEX as a revealed-preference layer on top of the standardized chain. Standard options show where liquidity is continuously quoted; FLEX shows where some participant wanted a payoff that the standard chain did not naturally provide.






The main limitations are sample size, non-random treatment timing, missing true market-cap data, missing dealer-signed inventory, and aggregate rather than leg-level option execution data. Future work should add market capitalization, institutional ownership, short interest, borrow costs, earnings controls, exact ATM option quotes, intraday quote timestamps, dealer/customer signs, and an out-of-sample design. Even with these limitations, the evidence is enough to show that FLEX is empirically measurable and economically relevant. The paper’s role is to establish the first layer of evidence and to define the research object clearly: FLEX is not just an institutional customization tool, but a public signal about where customized nonlinear risk is being created and where that risk may interact with regular markets.

This paper examines the evolution of moneylending in the face of intensifying competition between socially motivated MFIs. We develop a dynamic model of ex-post moral hazard where repayment is enforced through the threat of future credit exclusion. Our analysis identifies a critical functional complementarity: moneylenders leverage their informational and other advantages to provide “bridge loans” when MFI-funded projects fail, allowing borrowers to maintain MFI access. This symbiosis helps explain the persistence of high-interest moneylending despite global MFI expansion.






We demonstrate that MFI competition affects credit markets through two diverging channels. First, competition can weaken dynamic incentives by making exclusion less consequential, thereby tightening MFI credit constraints and reducing the amount lent by both MFIs and moneylenders. Second, borrowers may shift to MFIs for bridge loans. Despite such bridge-loans also being susceptible to moral hazard, we show that aggregate MFI loans increase, while moneylender loans go to zero. Consequently, while MFI competition consistently erodes the moneylender’s market share, its impact on total MFI lending remains theoretically ambiguous.






This framework also contributes to the longstanding debate on whether MFI and moneylender loans are substitutes or complements (e.g., 
Banerjee et al. (2015b)
; 
Banerjee et al. (2025)

MFI entry into underserved markets substitutes productive lending away from moneylenders, whereas in already-served markets moneylender bridge loans can be complementary to productive MFI lending. When MFIs themselves provide bridge finance, however, they directly substitute for moneylenders.






We test this prediction using a cluster-randomized trial in Bangladesh, where the randomized entry of an additional MFI into already-served villages increased local competition. Moneylender borrowing—consistent with the model—declines, reflected in fewer loans and lower total amounts, while MFI borrowing is unaffected. Effects on moneylender interest rates are inconclusive.






These insights carry two main policy implications. First, socially motivated MFIs may achieve greater impact by expanding into underserved areas rather than competing in saturated markets. Second, credit bureaus can help sustain both formal and informal lending in competitive markets by mitigating ex-post moral hazard 
(
Luoto et al., 2007
; 
De Janvry et al., 2010
)
. More broadly, our findings demonstrate how competition can reshape imperfect credit markets by weakening repayment incentives.

title: Cross-species representation learning aligns mouse and human neural dynamics and tracks clinical drug efficacy
hypothesis: However, its high dimensionality makes it difficult to distinguish conserved disease-related features from variation arising from species, recording modality and experimental context. Here, we test whether shared neural dynamics can be identified directly from electrophysiology data by learning representations organized by biological state rather than species. Across these three settings we test whether cross-species representation learning can identify conserved neural dynamics, capture clinically-relevant disease heterogeneity, and relate drug effects in mice to clinical outcomes.

3  Discussion




Here we show that cross-species neural representation learning can recover biologically-meaningful dimensions of neural activity that generalize between mice and humans despite substantial differences in species, recording modality and experimental context. Across increasingly challenging settings, the framework (1) recovered conserved sensory responses, (2) resolved distinct relationships between experimental epilepsy models and individual patients, and (3) identified convergent disease structure across genetically-distinct neurodevelopmental disorders. Most importantly, the frozen cross-species representation recovered the relative clinical efficacy of the tested interventions from drug-induced changes in mouse neural dynamics, without requiring any drug-response data for training or recalibration. These findings support the construction of a common biological coordinate system in which preclinical perturbations are evaluated by their relevance to human neural physiology.






This approach offers a novel perspective on the translational validity of animal models. Preclinical models are commonly evaluated according to how well they reproduce a disease as a whole
57
, yet heterogeneous neurological disorders are unlikely to correspond to a single experimental phenotype
58
. In epilepsy, PTZ, AY9944 and 4-AP occupied distinguishable regions of the learned disease space, and individual patients varied substantially in their affinity to each model. The relevant question may therefore be which patients, or which dimensions of their disease, a given model represents. With sufficiently diverse preclinical models, this could turn model selection into an empirical mapping problem in which experimental systems provide complementary coverage of human disease heterogeneity. The 
Fmr1
-16p11.2 analysis extends this idea further: translational correspondence need not require matched genetic aetiology, provided distinct perturbations converge on related circuit dynamics. Neural representations may therefore offer a means of organizing disease by functional pathophysiology rather than diagnosis or genotype alone
59
.






The same geometry provides a way to evaluate therapeutic efficacy. Conventional preclinical endpoints establish whether a treatment modifies an animal phenotype, but cannot determine whether the rescued feature is among those that are relevant to patients (Supplementary Figure 
2
). Here, efficacy can instead be expressed as displacement towards a human-anchored healthy state. The opposite effects of tiagabine in PTZ and the absence-like AY9944 model illustrate why this distinction matters. The pharmacological effect of an intervention depends on the disease dynamics in which it acts. More broadly, the latent space describes treatment response in more than one dimension. Movement along the conserved disease-to-healthy trajectory tracked therapeutic efficacy, whereas orthogonal displacement showed a weaker relationship with clinical secondary effects. This second result is exploratory. If it holds, cross-species representations would separate therapeutic normalization from other pharmacological effects within a single coordinate system.






The next extension is prediction of therapeutic response for individual patients. Our results show that individual patients exhibit varying degrees of alignment with experimentally tractable disease states, while pharmacological interventions differ in their ability to restore healthy neural dynamics within those same states. Combining these two relationships suggests a potential route to personalized treatment prediction: matching individual patients to the preclinical disease states that most closely resemble their neural dynamics and identifying the interventions that most effectively restore healthy activity within those states
60
, 
61
, 
62
. In this formulation, therapeutic prediction becomes an out-of-sample, or effectively zero-shot, inference problem rather than conventional supervised prediction from large cohorts of treated patients. Such an approach could also support clinical-trial enrichment by identifying patients whose baseline neural state most closely resembles the preclinical state in which a therapy produces rescue
60
, 
61
, 
62
. The present study establishes the foundation for this approach. Prospective prediction of treatment response in individual patients is the next step.






Several limitations define the scope of these conclusions. The pharmacological analysis was restricted to ten model-drug combinations and relied on retrospective clinical efficacy estimates rather than prospectively-collected human responses. Furthermore, the clinical efficacy benchmark combined interventions evaluated across different epilepsy syndromes and clinical endpoints. The epilepsy representation showed modest human disease discrimination, and AY9944 was weakly separated from control in the unified space, emphasizing that cross-species alignment cannot recover biological information that is poorly represented in the source datasets. External validation across recording systems, additional disease models and substantially larger intervention panels will therefore be important. A further conceptual limitation is the assumption that successful therapy moves neural activity towards an average healthy state. Effective interventions may instead produce compensatory neural states that restore function without reproducing untreated healthy dynamics. Future approaches will then need richer representations of the healthy and disease manifolds rather than a single restorative axis. Nevertheless, these findings support a shift in the central question of translational pharmacology: from asking whether a drug rescues an animal phenotype to determining which components of its therapeutic effects are conserved across species and relevant to human clinical efficacy. Scaling this framework across diverse preclinical models, pharmacological perturbations and human populations could make preclinical drug development a patient-anchored prediction problem, linking experimentally tractable neural states to individualized therapeutic responses in humans.

In doing so, we aim to capture two distinct aspects of neural systems that complicate straightforward hierarchical models of the brain. 1) That the brain consists of multiple interrelated interacting physical structures that engage in information processing in distinct but not entirely hierarchical ways. 2) That the brain operates at multiple timescales and these influence behavior. While an unknown (n) number of drivers could play a role here and across multiple biophysical systems, below we illustrate the concept by discussing the 3 concepts emphasized in this paper so far: effects across information enthalpy maximization, free-energy minimization and a drive to remain in a critical regime while processing information.








5.3 
Relationship between Information Entropy, Information Enthalpy and Neural Criticality




We posit that the state of a neural system can be mapped through the continuous interplay between information entropy and information enthalpy. Conversely, high entropy signals, such as 
random

structured
 signals, is necessary to drive neural adaptation, while remaining within the system’s available adaptive capacity. Therefore, we hypothesize that a neural system is in an 
optimal

We hypothesize that maintaining a sufficiently high information enthalpy provides the system with the capacity to acquire and retain useful predictive information about its environment, thereby supporting the complex internal dynamics required to remain near criticality. We hypothesize that an optimal information enthalpy regime, characterized by a sufficiently high predictive-information capacity supported by abundant, high-quality and non-redundant information, provides favorable conditions for maintaining critical-like dynamics. We propose that such informational assistance may also influence functional connectivity and facilitate the emergence of complex adaptive behaviors. In future work, we aim to empirically investigate the impact of high-IEP input on neural dynamics to empirically evaluate these theoretical predictions.
conclusion:
6 
Discussion




This paper attempts to tackle one of the most ambitious scientific questions still facing humankind: what leads a collection of cells to be able to self-organize, adopt states, and persist across decades in such a way as to display general intelligence potent enough to reshape the environment that gave rise to it? Or more simply: how does intelligence arise from a brain? In asking this question we face the paradox proposed nearly 90 years ago by Emerson M. Pugh: 
“If the human brain were so simple that we could understand it, we would be so simple that we couldn’t”
. Naturally this paper does not answer these questions fully. However, we believe it establishes a conceptual stepping stone. The ideas here can be tested by combining advancements across mathematics, computing, biology and bioengineering, electrical engineering, and emerging fields like Synthetic Biological Intelligence (SBI) that seek to leverage simplified neural systems for information processing and intelligence. If the theory presented here has merit, key falsifiable implications have already arisen. For the sake of brevity, we make explicit four key examples here: 1) Increasing the 
IEP
\mathrm{IEP}
 of sensory input, while holding firing-rate statistics approximately fixed, should move neural dynamics toward canonical signatures of criticality, up to saturation imposed by capacity and biological costs; 2) The sensitivity of criticality metrics to changes in input structure should peak near the boundary between ordered and disordered regimes; 3) Reductions in effective throughput capacity 
C
r
,
t
C_{\mathrm{r,t}}
 should weaken both information enthalpy accumulation and the stability of critical-like dynamics, even under highly structured input; and 4) The n-body formulation should provide a more effective physics-based constraint to shape the neurocomputational dynamics of biological neural networks when the information entropy and information enthalpy of input signals is constrained in particular ways. Some of these implications are relatively simple to test and others require additional technological advancement to confidently explore.






An implicit aspect of the information enthalpy formulation presented here was that this is proposed as a complementary and interacting normative principle for active inference with that of the FEP. Many of the same properties that make active inference compelling as a theoretical basis become stronger by the addition of a second normative principle that potentially operates via different neural mechanisms. The broad processes of actively sampling and predicting the environment and associated outcomes of actions remain; however, based on the requirements of the neural system carrying out these processes, what the actions or predictions will aim to optimize will vary. This simplifies accounts in FEP literature that currently require complex generative models to explain behavior. Arguably however, this model would better accord with earlier conceptions that suggested aversions to “dark rooms”, self-induced instabilities (sometimes called “autovitiation”), and similar features, were essentially due to predetermined genetic priors. Here, these genetic priors are made explicit, but under a separate and competing driver from that described in the FEP. In this case, the priors are established by the driver to maximize the amount of usable information that a system collects. Future work will have to further explore this relationship, especially through well controlled experimentation.






Finally, while this paper makes great efforts to introduce in detail the information enthalpy driver and to contrast this new theoretical concept against the established FEP-based free-energy minimization concept, we do not propose that other drivers do not exist. This is why we introduce the notion that there is an inherent driver for criticality in neural systems, as previous work suggests this is a self-organizing feature of dynamic systems embodied within a structured information landscape where information storage and transfer is a requirement 
[
62
]
. What is likely however, is that there are primary and secondary drivers to neural systems. In this case, we would propose information enthalpy maximization and free-energy minimization are primary drivers, while neural criticality maintenance are secondary drivers. Functionally, this would work similarly to an astrophysics n-body formulation, where the impact of individual bodies on the whole system will differ based on the mass of each system, due to the different gravitational forces. The n-body-inspired framework presented here aims to provide a conceptualization for systems with distinct drivers may interact to produce changes in neural state spaces as a result of conflicting forces, even if detailing exact biophysical system level interactions that might drive the system as a whole is beyond the scope of this (already extensive) manuscript. Fortunately however, the benefit in the approach here is that, under controlled conditions, the dynamics of these different drivers as they may apply to different biophysical system can be measured, manipulated, and the theoretical perspective then updated. By exploring across scales and complexity, this iterative approach offers the best chance to understand how the brain works to give rise to intelligence, or at the very least, that of a simple brain.

title: CircuitATLAS: Agentic reasoning over a systems neuroscience knowledge graph for target discovery in circuitopathies
hypothesis:

conclusion:
6  Discussion




Here, we introduce CircuitATLAS, a framework for CNS target discovery that
begins with disease-associated neural activity phenotypes and identifies
molecular interventions capable of shifting pathological circuits toward more
functional states. We constructed a provenance-linked systems-neuroscience
knowledge graph integrating published literature, human molecular atlases, and
newly generated 
in vivo
 experimental data. Building on this, we developed an
evidence-gated agentic workflow that connects neural activity phenotypes to
their circuit and cellular substrates and identifies molecular effectors capable
of modulating them. We further established a human-governed lab-in-the-loop
framework linking target nomination to experimental design, execution and
validation. Together, this establishes a therapeutic discovery approach in which
molecular targets are selected for their capacity to correct circuit
dysfunction, irrespective of whether they are themselves altered in disease.






Recent advances in protein structure prediction
41
, molecular generation
and protein design
42
 are progressively lowering the barrier between a
specified biological target and a candidate therapeutic, making target
identification and validation an increasingly important bottleneck. As more of
the proteome becomes technically addressable, therapeutic discovery may become
less constrained by the availability of interventions than by our ability to
identify which biological nodes are most consequential to perturb. CircuitATLAS
provides a systematic way to prioritize these targets by integrating evidence
across biological scales.






This work also belongs to a broader shift from biomedical knowledge retrieval
toward scientific reasoning systems. Knowledge graphs such as SPOKE
15
,
TxGNN
18
 and more recent systems such as PROTON
43
 have demonstrated
the value of organizing heterogeneous biomedical relationships for prediction
and hypothesis generation. Agentic systems are increasingly extending this idea
from retrieval to multistep scientific workflows
44,45
; ROBIN
46
, for
example, coupled literature reasoning and experimental analysis to generate and
test biological hypotheses. CircuitATLAS differs principally in the
representation chosen for the problem. Electrophysiological features, circuits,
regions and cell populations are explicit intermediate objects rather than
contextual annotations around molecular disease associations. Our agentic
workflow then constrains reasoning through these intermediate levels, including
deliberately masking disease-molecule relationships during target generation to
reduce shortcut reasoning.






The potential of CircuitATLAS ultimately lies in combining literature-scale
knowledge (Figure 1) with large volumes of standardized experimental data
(Figures 2 and 3). Published studies provide a valuable record of existing scientific
knowledge, but are subject to publication bias, underreporting of negative
results, and incomplete documentation of the experimental conditions that
influence neural measurements. This is particularly consequential in systems
neuroscience, where minor sources of variation can change both neural and
pharmacological phenotypes
47
. Addressing this variability requires more
standardized approaches to neural data generation, including consistent
acquisition hardware, experimental protocols, metadata collection, and analysis
pipelines, together with systematic reporting of negative results. Such
standardization would enable more direct comparisons of neural phenotypes and
intervention effects across disease models and experiments. CircuitATLAS
provides a common representation in which these newly generated observations can
be integrated with existing literature-derived evidence. As experimental
datasets accumulate, these initially heuristic weights could themselves be
calibrated against prospective outcomes, allowing the graph to learn not only
more biology, but which kinds of evidence are most predictive of successful
intervention.






Similarly, as agent-guided intervention-outcome datasets grow, the

lab-in-the-loop
 could evolve into a genuine learning system.
Closed-loop laboratories in chemistry and protein engineering have already shown
how active learning or reinforcement-learning-style policies can use previous
experiments to select increasingly informative subsequent experiments
48,49
.
In 
in vivo
 neuroscience, however, noisy observations, slow experiments and ethical
costs make human oversight essential, which is why approval by a named
scientist sits between the agent’s proposal and any animal work.






Several limitations remain. First, the central translational assumption is that
disease-relevant circuit phenotypes and their corrective directions are
sufficiently conserved between experimental models and humans. Human
systems-neuroscience datasets remain comparatively sparse and rarely permit
causal perturbation; molecular atlases
30
 can establish that candidate
effectors are present in the relevant human cells, but not that manipulating
them will produce the same circuit-level response across species. Second,
CircuitATLAS is constrained by the evidence from which it is built. The
literature is biased toward well-studied diseases, positive findings and
experimentally accessible mechanisms, while deterministic entity resolution and
relation extraction inevitably omit or misclassify some evidence. Although
provenance and inference-time verification make individual reasoning chains
auditable, they do not eliminate these limitations. Third, the performance of
the discovery system itself has not yet been established prospectively. The
examples presented here demonstrate that CircuitATLAS can generate biologically
plausible hypotheses and, for ATP1A3, nominate a target subsequently validated

in vivo
, but they do not establish its success rate, relative performance against
expert-led or alternative computational approaches, or ability to predict
therapeutic efficacy across indications. Several prospective, preregistered
campaigns will therefore be required to determine whether accumulating
experimental outcomes improve target prioritization and experimental efficiency
over time.






CircuitATLAS provides a framework for discovering therapeutic targets through
their capacity to control pathological neural circuits. By combining structured
knowledge, agentic reasoning and iterative experimentation, it offers a path
toward systematically identifying biological control points capable of restoring
brain function.

title: Cross-Validation of Open-Source Quantum Network Simulators
hypothesis:
Before describing the quantum network simulators in detail, we give a brief overview in terms of design and implementation choices. We aim to help the reader choose the appropriate tool for their requirements, because as shown in Section 
VI
, both simulators produce similar results.
conclusion:
Discussion




We have performed a cross-validation of QuISP and SeQUeNCe, two prominent open-source simulators for quantum networks.
We studied the protocols that both simulators use to generate link-level entanglement in order to evaluate how long each simulator takes to satisfy a connection request.
QuISP relies on a protocol requiring fewer classical messages, leading to faster rate of link-level entanglement compared to SeQUeNCe.
Interestingly, we discovered that the slower connection setup protocol for SeQUeNCe is insensitive to the placement of the BSA node, a property that might be of interest when planning deployment of first generation quantum networks.






We also focused on how the simulators handle noisy operations and decoherence of quantum memories in both entanglement swapping and purification scenarios.
The simulators agreed on the general qualitative behavior but differed on the specific values of end-to-end fidelity.
This can be understood by the different communication models utilized by both simulators. The interplay between differences in both communication models and error models will be explored in more detail as future work.






The tests presented here have strengthened our confidence in both simulators and deepened our understanding of the performance impact of the differences in the modeled protocols. The tests described in this paper are deliberately chosen to also be analytically tractable, allowing us to write down closed-form equations, which match the outcomes of the simulations. With these results in hand, the obvious next step is to move beyond analytically tractable cases and compare the results of larger and more complex systems.
Examples of such systems include longer chains of quantum repeaters with complex entanglement swapping and purification policies, different link architectures, and different quantum repeater generations. Our cross-validation experiments also pave the way to benchmarking quantum networks with non-trivial topologies as well as multiplexed networks servicing multiple independent connection requests simultaneously.






Despite the existence of suites of software quality assurance (SQA) tests for both simulators, this exercise has not only given us a deeper understanding of the network design choices but also resulted in numerous outright bug fixes to both simulators. We recommend this direct comparison approach for both quantum and classical network simulators where possible.

In this paper, we introduce new robust portfolio selection models by incorporating a reward and penalty mechanism into portfolio management. These models also serve as frameworks that balance portfolio loss and the associated downside risk in portfolio management. To determine optimal allocations for these models, we derive an explicit closed-form expression for the worst-case CVaR under the reward-penalty mechanism. AlphaFold 3 uses the MSA as a shortcut to predict nonlocal structural features. Without the MSA, the model retains much of the predicted local secondary structure but fails to predict the long-range contacts and partnerships required to organize a correct fold. Restoring the MSA-enriched pair representations of just 40 residues—roughly 10–15% of a typical chain—recovers a median of 71% of the lost experimental accuracy. The necessary information in the MSA is therefore distributed, partially redundant, and remarkably sparse. It does not reside in a privileged set of residues, nor does it require the complete MSA-enriched state to attain high recovery.






The Pairformer subsequently reorganizes this MSA-derived contribution. By block 25, a component wholly orthogonal to the original MSA-aligned component dominates the internal representation. Yet this reorganization does not prevent the emergence of the fold; rather, it accompanies it. Probing the pair representation directly shows that, with the MSA, the global fold becomes decodable by block 9 of the 48-block pass in aggregate.






Without the MSA, no protein has an emergent fold by that point, and only 14% do by the end of the first Pairformer pass. The Pairformer, thus, does not merely propagate the MSA’s contribution. It rapidly transforms a compact evolutionary signal into an extractable representation of the predicted global fold, which the remainder of the pass then refines, and which the diffusion module ultimately decodes into coordinates.






The intermediate diffusion readouts show what this transformation looks like to the model’s own structural decoder. The earliest diffusion structures are overcompact and featureless, with helices appearing before strands and exact

With the full MSA, the global fold emerges within roughly the first ten blocks. With small, evolutionarily diverse subsets, it takes about thirty-six blocks, even though both arrive at the correct-fold regime by the end of the first pass; the subsets primarily miss some of the finer relationships supplied by the complete alignment. The MSA also influences the initial direction of the trajectory: different sets of homologs generate distinct early emergence pathways much more readily than different query sequences do. If the query sequence matters chiefly by encoding a structure, if different sets of homologs separate the trajectory more than different queries do, and if members of a fold family converge only when an alignment is present, then what the model draws from the alignment may not be the evolutionary relationship between those sequences and the query at all, but the structure that relationship happens to encode. If that were so, an alignment assembled for an entirely different protein should serve just as well, provided the two proteins share a fold and the alignment is supplied at the target’s structurally corresponding residues.

Supplying a protein with only the structurally aligned columns of a different protein’s alignment, with every other column gapped, raises the median TM-score against experiment from 0.442 to 0.717 in Sabmark pairs sharing 9% sequence identity, and from 0.568 to 0.762 in post-cutoff proteins that could not have been seen during training. Overwriting only those columns in a protein’s own working alignment is similarly destructive.






What the model requires is therefore structural information in the correct register. The alignment is not merely evolutionary evidence from which AlphaFold infers a fold, but a transferable description of structure that the model can read directly when supplied in the correct register.






Our results suggest that the conventional reading of AlphaFold’s success, that the model has largely solved structure prediction and that the alignment is a helpful but secondary input, therefore has it backwards. The alignment does not seem to be a hint that the model exploits. Rather, it is where the fold comes from. Without it, the model does not merely do worse—it fails to arrive at a global fold at all within a complete Pairformer pass, and even ten rounds of recycling leave it short of the threshold for a correct fold

22
, 
25

It reads the arrangement from its input and spends the remainder of the computation refining what it was given. Seen this way the behavior is not surprising. A model trained to minimize structural error, given inputs that reliably encode the answer, has no reason to learn to derive from sequence what it can read from an alignment.






This is the titular shortcut: not a shortcut from evolutionary history to structure, but a shortcut from the structure already latent in an alignment to the structure the model outputs. It is extraordinarily effective, and nothing in these results diminishes that. But its effectiveness is also the reason the problem is not closed. Frontier models such as ESMFold2 
[
36
]
 and OpenDDE 
[
37
]

Until a model can recover protein structure confidently and accurately from sequence alone, without an input that already encodes much of the fold, we do not believe the underlying problem has been solved.






If the model is indeed reading structure from the alignment, the finding also changes what one might do with that fact. Alignment depth has long been treated as a fundamental constraint, and orphan proteins, designed sequences, and fast-evolving families are hard cases because few homologs can be found. Our results suggest the constraint is structural rather than evolutionary, meaning that the provided alignment need not be the protein’s own evolutionary history but some other protein’s with a similar fold. Where a structural hypothesis exists—from a biophysical argument, a partial model, or a low-resolution experiment—it may be possible to construct an alignment that conveys it. The same logic applies to conformational heterogeneity. MSA subsampling is currently used to coax alternative conformations from the model by removing sequences and observing what changes 
[

39

But they follow from the mechanism, and they are not available under the view that the alignment’s value lies in its evolutionary relationship to the query.






These findings also carry a lesson beyond structure prediction. Predictive accuracy alone does not reveal the computation that produces it, and a model may achieve accurate outputs by exploiting information already present in its inputs rather than by reproducing the process it is used to study. Causal interventions on internal representations, together with readouts of intermediate states, make it possible to distinguish the two, and we expect them to be equally informative for other biological models whose accuracy has outpaced our understanding of how it is achieved.

The present work investigated a thermal transmission problem in a film-bulk domain, considering both a finite-thickness film configuration and the corresponding thin-film limit. 6  Conclusion




In credit risk modelling, the LGD risk parameter is commonly modelled by following a two-stage loan-level modelling approach. Each stage corresponds to a separate
component model (write-off risk and the loss severity), and the product thereof constitutes the expected loss. The rationale of such a modelling strategy is that it can faithfully recover the typical shape of the empirical LGD-distribution. This LGD-distribution is commonly characterised by bimodality and a heavy skew in its tails, owing to the dominance of zero-valued cures.
However, some banks employ an approach based on a 
run-off triangle
 (ROT) from the actuarial science literature in modelling the LGD at the portfolio-level. This modelling strategy is a relatively understudied topic within the context of credit risk modelling. It is certainly true that some synergies exist between insurance loss data and credit loss data that would seemingly support following this ROT-based approach. However, the ROT-based approach also has a slew of demerits, as we have discussed in the appendix. These demerits make the approach intractable when compared to the more established 
regression-based
 LGD-modelling approach that is trained at the loan-level. Perhaps the greatest of these demerits is the inability of a ROT-based LGD-modelling approach to produce loan-level LGD-estimates. The natural question then arises: which approach is ‘best’ in producing the most credible and accurate LGD-estimates given empirical loss data?
It is in this context that we conduct an in-depth comparative study between a loan-level LGD-modelling strategy and a ROT-based one towards filling the obvious gap in literature.






In our study, we formulated two variants of a ROT-based LGD-model that are largely based on industry experience. These variants include a single-stage model and a more sophisticated two-stage model, which decomposes the expected loss into a write-off risk component and a loss severity component (or triangles). Both of these ROT-based LGD-models are then compared against a classical two-stage regression-based LGD-model. The two components within this regression-based LGD-model are estimated using simple modelling techniques, which includes binary logistic regression for write-off risk, and a Gaussian GLM for the loss severity. We purposefully selected these techniques for their simplicity and ubiquity in banking, without reaching for more sophisticated modelling techniques such as those from the machine learning literature.
In so doing, we believe that our comparative study is fairer to the simple ROT-based approach, without compromising our subsequent findings.






We fitted the two variants of the ROT-based LGD-modelling approach to a portfolio of credit card data from a large South African bank, and note the following main demerits and general findings.
The aggregation logic of the ROT-based approach is sensitive to extreme observations, which demonstrably affects the downstream LGD-estimates. We know from literature that the ROT-based approach is also prone to becoming over-parametrised relative to the available data, which is further compounded when segmenting the data prior to estimating a ROT within each segment. Furthermore, the recursive estimation of development factors (and therefore subsequent forecasts) are prone to error propagation whereby bias in earlier cell-estimates can be carried forward into forecasting each new ROT-cell. In reality, these development factors are also not necessarily stable across default cohorts, which violates a key assumption of the ROT-based approach.
Lastly, compiling LGD-values over time (default date) when following this approach amounts to blending the concepts of ‘empirical’ and ‘expected’ quantities, especially as one moves to more recent default cohorts. This operation complicates model assessment, which can easily hoodwink the practitioner into thinking that the completed ROT fits the loss experience well. We found otherwise, having explicitly compared the ‘forecast’ time series of ROT-based LGD-values against the mean empirical loss rate over time. Specifically, we found substantial divergence between these two rate pairs, which further brings into question the overall tractability of the ROT-based approach to LGD-modelling; as critically discussed in the appendix.






Using the same data, we developed a regression-based LGD-model that consists of two component models: the 
probability of write-off given default
 (PWGD) model, and the 
loss given write-off
 (LGW) model.
Both component models are assessed individually, and our assessment spans a number of diagnostics and modelling aspects, e.g., discriminatory power (ROC-analysis), predictive accuracy (Brier scores), and distributional analyses. Accordingly, each component model fits the data well and produces credible and sufficiently accurate predictions of the loss experience (or elements thereof).
Having built our regression-based LGD-model, we finally compared the aggregated LGD-estimates from each approach to the mean empirical rate over time. Our results indicate that both ROT-based approaches exhibit significant divergence from the empirical rate. In contrast, the regression-based approach produces aggregates that closely follow the time-sensitive trends in the empirical rate, which clearly underscores greater prediction accuracy. This result also suggests that the underlying regression-based LGD-model has a greater ability to adapt to changing portfolio and economic conditions, relative to the ROT-based LGD-model(s).
Therefore, our work demonstrably showcases the benefits of a loan-level modelling strategy, even when using relatively simple modelling techniques in estimating each component. By implication,
a loan-level regression-based approach to estimating the LGD risk parameter is probably better than using a portfolio-level ROT-based approach.






Future work can explore other techniques for completing a ROT, and then repeat the comparative study. Whilst we have opted to use the simple and ubiquitous chain-ladder technique in completing a ROT, other techniques (e.g., the Bornhuetter-Ferguson technique) may produce different LGD-estimates over time.
While data availability is typically problematic, the study could also be reperformed on other credit datasets and/or on portfolios other than credit cards. Doing so can help generalise our findings. Furthermore, our regression-based LGD-model serves as a foundational basis on which future research can improve. It is certainly possible to replace the modelling technique that underpins the PWGD and LGW models with more sophisticated techniques, whereafter the comparative study can be reperformed. Doing so would likely engender greater predictive accuracy in the LGD-estimates, thereby strengthening the case for moving away from ROT-based LGD-models.

title: Latent Continuum of Regimes in Limit Order Book Dynamics
hypothesis:
Abstract


Market-regime models typically assume a finite set of discrete latent states. We examine whether high
frequency limit-order-book dynamics exhibit distinct regime separation or apparent regimes result from
discretising an underlying continuum of market conditions.
conclusion:
9 
Conclusion




Markets may move continuously even when the models used to describe them do
not. For the deep limit order book examined here, conventional market regimes
appear less like naturally separated states and more like convenient
partitions of a continuously evolving stress process. This distinction matters: imposing labels too early
can turn gradual movement into artificial transitions, conceal meaningful
variation within categories, and produce boundaries that appear convincing in
sample but fail as market conditions change.






The hierarchical results show that broad bands can usefully summarise market
stress, but finer classifications increasingly distort the underlying
continuum, replacing meaningful distance and direction with unstable
boundaries that improve in-sample separation while weakening out-of-sample
prediction. This explains the apparent success and eventual failure of
discrete classifications.






The continuous representation preserves ordering
without relying on unstable boundaries. Predictive information shifts
smoothly between slow and fast components as the decomposition timescale
changes, with no privileged boundary between macro and micro dynamics, while
the residual analysis shows that the state is not strictly one-dimensional.
The micro-subspace adds significant predictive value, with the largely linear
forecasting relationship indicating that this information originates from the
covariance state, not model complexity.
Discrete micro-regimes do not recover this information,
confirming that the loss cannot be repaired merely by adding more hierarchical
labels. Even a carefully constructed hierarchy therefore cannot fully
represent a state space whose predictive structure changes smoothly.






Our research provides a practical approach showing how continuous and discrete
representations can complement each other in regime detection and where each
is most appropriate. The relevant transition is not a universal time cutoff,
but the point at which discretisation improves operational clarity without
sacrificing stability or predictive information. Rather than choosing a regime
count in advance, research should focus on comparing geometric evidence,
boundary stability, chronological transfer, and predictive loss across
observation and forecast horizons. A discrete representation is justified where broad partitions
remain stable and transfer out of sample; a continuous representation is
preferable where predictive information survives in the coordinate but
disappears after classification. The transition from a continuous to a
discrete representation must be identified empirically across timescales, not
imposed as a modelling assumption. This perspective has direct
applications beyond regime classification. In simulation, continuous state
dynamics can generate gradual stress accumulation, mean reversion, and
realistic movement between market conditions without artificial jumps between
labels. In risk management, the dial can support live monitoring of market
stress while discrete thresholds remain available for escalation and
communication. On trading desks, it could condition execution, hedging,
exposure, or liquidity decisions on both the current stress level and the
rate at which conditions are changing. Tracking a continuous path may reduce
the delayed reactions and unstable signal switching produced when observations
repeatedly cross rigid regime boundaries. These applications require
dedicated economic evaluation and should not be interpreted as evidence of
trading profitability from the present study.






Future research will develop continuous-regime detection methods that
distinguish ordinary movement, temporary displacement, and structural change,
and test whether the observed structure generalises across markets and crisis
periods. This will help establish when the continuum persists and when
genuinely discrete behaviour emerges.






This research contributes to a broader shift in how market regimes are
understood.
Once the focus shifts from assigning labels to measuring how market conditions
evolve and how their representation transitions from continuous to discrete,
the whole vocabulary of regimes changes. The central question therefore
changes from “Which state is the market in?” to “Where is the market on the

Astrocytes are increasingly recognized as active regulators of neural dynamics, yet their role in large-scale synchronization remains incompletely understood. hypothesis: From this intuition, we expect the student to have higher entropy than the teacher; we now show that this does indeed hold at optimality.

Conclusion




The divergence used in distillation is often inherited rather than chosen: a sequence-level derivation ties reverse KL to on-policy data and forward KL to off-policy data.
Once we disentangled these choices, we found that the divergence, more than the sampling distribution, acts as an implicit regularizer on the student.
Forward KL inflates the entropy of the student above that of the teacher by exactly the residual divergence on average, so the entropy of a converged pretraining run can be read from its loss.
Reverse KL deflates entropy, but only as long as the student can mimic the teacher; whether it does is a property of the divergence and the task together, not of the divergence alone.
In between, and depending on how the tail of the distribution is handled, entropy can be tuned, smoothly early in training and abruptly at convergence.
These effects compound in self-distillation, where the teacher is derived from the student: any entropy drop feeds back into the next teacher, and the hyperparameters that work best are those whose inflation counteracts the drop that conditioning on privileged information induces.






Practically, our results suggest choosing the sampling distribution and the divergence separately, and treating the latter as an entropy knob rather than as a consequence of the former.






We obtained these results with a toy model of language modeling, simple enough to admit precise mathematical statements yet rich enough to reproduce key phenomena at scale.
We hope that it will replace the Gaussian mixtures inherited from variational inference as the go-to example to reason about distillation in large language models, and that it will prove useful beyond entropy.

Uncertainty provides meaningful information about semantic correctness in diffusion-based CECT synthesis, and can additionally identify clinically relevant out-of-distribution cases. Among the methods evaluated, MCDropout emerges as the method of choice: it performs strongly at every scale and under distribution shift, and requires no additional training when the base model already contains dropout, making it the practical default. BayesDiff places a posterior on the final convolutional layer alone,
treating all preceding layers as a fixed feature extractor, so its
uncertainty reflects one layer rather than the full denoiser — a
plausible explanation for its consistently weak performance and its
negative region-level correlation. Ensemble and HyperDiff instead
capture variability across the entire network, and HyperDiff
concentrates it within spatially coherent regions, consistent with its
region-level strength. MCDropout produces many closely related
subnetworks whose disagreement varies smoothly across neighbouring

deployment.

Discussion




In the present work, we first derived a geometry that satisfies the requirements set out at the outset: a modular structure based on a topologically interlocked assembly composed of three distinct block types, capable of being expanded, and enclosing a usable internal volume. This geometry was then evaluated under the expected lunar environmental conditions, both in the complete assembly and in three configurations where one block was removed. We demonstrated that a habitat based on topological interlocking is feasible and that the structure retains a significant degree of integrity even when individual blocks are missing. This confirms one of the principal advantages of topological interlocking: inherent tolerance of TI structures to localised failure or loss of a module.






In addition, the proposed construction method enables a more holistic lightweighting strategy through in‑situ resource utilisation (ISRU). Current approaches are often constrained by the size of the habitat to be constructed on the Moon or require the entire structure to be delivered from Earth, resulting in substantial mass penalties. By contrast, the present approach allows the bulk of the structural material to be sourced directly on the lunar surface.






Several assumptions underlie the present work, the most significant concerning the material properties of lunar regolith. Although terrestrial analogue materials have been shown in the literature to be sinterable, the resulting material properties may differ substantially from those of actual lunar regolith.






In addition, the habitat proposed in this work does not yet incorporate provisions for entry and exit, and a dedicated system for this purpose might need to be transported from Earth. Such a system might be integrated within a TIA‑based design, but this lies outside the scope of the present study.






Furthermore, we assume the presence of a membrane to ensure gas‑tightness. This design measure is necessary because the geometry of TIAs, with gaps between the blocks, does not provide a hermetic enclosure of the internal volume, and these gaps may further change under load. The authors are not aware of existing research on the gas‑tightness of TIA‑based structures, and this aspect of habitat design will need to be addressed in future work.






Lastly, the proposed habitat is based on an existing geometry with only minor modifications. TIAs possess a large number of parameters that determine the exact block geometry, and a purpose‑optimised design, tailored entirely to the requirements of a lunar habitat, might perform even better.






In summary, this work demonstrates numerically that it is feasible to construct a habitat based on TIAs, which - given current understanding of the available material - can be realised largely through ISRU. The design accommodates the inherent brittleness of sintered regolith and enables the internal pressurisation loads to be carried effectively as well as future reuse of the constructed blocks through expansion.
